benchmarks.name: CoffeeBench
benchmarks.owner_year: Sakana AI with KPMG AZSA; June 2026 (arXiv 2606.16613)
benchmarks.format: Multi-agent coffee supply chain with 2 farmers, 2 roasters and 2 retailers. The model under test runs one roaster. The other five firms are fixed reference agents (Claude Sonnet 4.6), and firms message and trade with each other.
benchmarks.measures: Whether a mid-chain firm can earn net income while negotiating and trading with LLM firms upstream and downstream.
benchmarks.scoring: Cumulative net income, averaged over 3 runs per model, compared with a passive baseline that takes no actions. The authors give a 'loose symmetric-duopoly' headroom of about $23,800 [S]. GPT-5.5 ranks first and Opus 4.7 second, and every model beats the passive baseline. Haiku 4.5 shows 'idle drift': its plans are coherent but it keeps choosing to do nothing [S].
benchmarks.multi_agent: Yes. One focal LLM plays against 5 reference firms that all run on Sonnet 4.6, in different economic roles.
weaknesses: Only 3 seeds per model, and the README says one run costs over $200 and takes over 5 hours [P].
The reference firms are LLMs, so opponents are not deterministic, and sharing a model family with the focal agent may help or hurt it [inference].
The authors call their headroom estimate loose and optimistic [S].
Not confirmed whether firms start with different capital or positions [S].
Per-model numbers not seen: arXiv and pub.sakana.ai were DNS-blocked.
sources: [P] https://github.com/SakanaAI/CoffeeBench (README: 90 days; 2/2/2 firms; 5 focal models x 3 seeds; over $200 and 5 h per run)
[S] https://pub.sakana.ai/coffeebench/ and arXiv 2606.16613, via search snippets (Sonnet 4.6 reference agents, GPT-5.5 > Opus 4.7, idle drift, ~$23,800 headroom)

benchmarks.name: RetailBench
benchmarks.owner_year: Ant Group and City University of Hong Kong (Zhang, Wang, Wu, Zhang); v1 March 2026 (arXiv 2603.16453), v2 June 2026 (arXiv 2606.15862)
benchmarks.format: Single-store supermarket simulation 'grounded in data', framed as a partially observable decision process. Tools cover pricing, replenishment, supplier choice, shelf assortment, inventory ageing, customer feedback, external events and cash-flow limits.
benchmarks.measures: Whether a decision policy stays coherent over a long horizon in retail operations.
benchmarks.scoring: Survival to the end of the horizon, plus final net worth and sales, compared with a privileged non-LLM oracle (one configuration: survives 180 days, net worth 131,510.42, 122 stockouts). Only a few of 7 LLMs (v2; 8 in v1) survive, and all trail the oracle by a wide margin [S].
weaknesses: The oracle sees structured simulator state, so it is an approximate upper bound, not a fair comparison [S].
The two versions differ in model count and framing [S].
One store and one configuration for the oracle [S].
Whether demand lost to stockouts is hidden from the agent is not stated in the snippets [S].
arXiv blocked; abstract-level only.
sources: [S] https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15862 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.16453, via search snippets
[S] https://pith.science/paper/2606.15862 (third-party review: oracle uses structured simulator fields)

benchmarks.name: MerchantBench
benchmarks.owner_year: Qiming Shi et al. (Zhejiang, Peking, Fudan); July 2026 (arXiv 2607.28956)
benchmarks.format: Seller-side e-commerce simulation at the level of individual orders. 98,843 real product records (36,576 suppliers on Alibaba 1688, per a secondary write-up) and 26 tools. Supplier events show up immediately, but order outcomes (fulfilment, delivery, settlement, after-sales) arrive late.
core_facets: agent framework as a factor (ReAct vs Hermes)
benchmarks.measures: Long-term coherence: sourcing, pricing, cash flow and reacting to feedback that arrives late.
benchmarks.scoring: Final net assets (headline), plus GMV, profit margin, sustained-window rate, store rating and fines [S]. 8 LLMs x 2 frameworks = 48 runs. The best configuration reaches 27.3% of the human participants' mean final net assets. GPT-5.6 Sol leads on assets under ReAct, Opus 4.8 has the best store rating, and GLM-5.2 handles the most orders but pays the most fines [S].
benchmarks.humans: 3 human participants with no e-commerce experience. The repo offers a 'human' browser playground on the same simulator [P].
weaknesses: The human baseline is only 3 people [S].
A third-party automated review flags a context-compression confound that the paper does not isolate [S].
The public repo ships only a synthetic data generator (1,000 products, 200 suppliers); 'real-world business data is not included' [P].
Implied 3 runs per model x framework [inference].
sources: [P] https://github.com/KhanCold/merchantbench (README: 365 days; delayed downstream outcomes; human playground; synthetic generator only; ReAct and Hermes)
[S] arXiv 2607.28956 abstract via search snippets; hyper.ai and aiweekly.co summaries (model results, 27.3%, 3 humans); pith.science review

benchmarks.name: EcoGym
benchmarks.format: Three economic environments behind one interface: Vending (an open re-implementation adapted from the closed Vending-Bench), Freelance and Operation.
benchmarks.measures: Long-horizon planning and execution in small economies.
benchmarks.scoring: Net worth (Vending), income (Freelance) and daily active users (Operation), mean ± SD over 3–5 runs. No single model of the 11 tested leads all three [S].
weaknesses: Numbers differ between paper versions and summaries (e.g. Vending net worth 1,843 vs 11,272 for different models and runs) [S].
No human or oracle reference was found.
The Vending environment is a reconstruction of a closed benchmark, so fidelity to Vending-Bench is unverified [inference].
sources: [S] https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.09514, via search snippets (arXiv HTML table excerpt; alphaxiv overview)

benchmarks.name: EnterpriseArena ('Can LLM Agents Be CFOs?')
benchmarks.owner_year: Yi Han et al.; March 2026 (arXiv 2603.23638), later revised
benchmarks.format: CFO simulator for a FinTech lending firm. The agent manages liquidity, closes the books, buys costly information signals and raises equity or debt as the macro environment changes. Built on transformed firm data, anonymised documents, macro and industry series, and operating rules validated by experts.
core_facets: partial observability via budgeted tools (20 calls/month)
benchmarks.measures: Long-horizon capital allocation under uncertainty; trading off paying for information against conserving resources.
benchmarks.scoring: Survival to the end of the horizon and financial outcomes. The newer version tests 23 LLMs x 4 agent frameworks: 15.4% of trials survive, and larger models are not reliably better (the earlier version reports 11 LLMs and 16%) [S].
benchmarks.multi_agent: No (the authors list the single-agent design as a limitation) [S].
weaknesses: Results depend on the version [S].
Single agent [S].
Expert-validated rules are not the same as validation against outcomes [inference].

benchmarks.name: Turing CEO Bench (Simulated Virtual Company)
benchmarks.format: A static simulated company workspace (SVC). Its first company, 'Cirrus Sleep, Inc.', is a direct-to-consumer brand with one complete fiscal year in 1,100+ files (accounting, HR, board materials, Slack history). Department-level and executive tasks are written by finance and operations practitioners.
benchmarks.measures: Reconciling conflicting data and making judgement calls on finance and operations work.
benchmarks.scoring: Not published in what we could see. 500+ tasks, of which 40 are published and scored; samples on request [S].
benchmarks.humans: Practitioners write the tasks; no human performance baseline seen.
weaknesses: Name collision: this is the third 'CEO bench' (Princeton CEO-Bench and the 'Can LLMs Be CEOs?' CEO-Bench, both in our notes) [S].
The world is static, with no dynamics or feedback loop [S].
Mostly private; scoring method unknown.
turing.com is DNS-blocked.

benchmarks.name: LemonadeBench
benchmarks.format: Lemonade stand: set the price, buy perishable supplies (lemons last 7 days, cups 30, sugar 60), choose opening hours; $1,000 start, $5/hour operating cost; demand Q = 50 − 10p with hourly variation.
benchmarks.measures: Basic economic intuition: price discovery, perishability, hours.
benchmarks.scoring: Profit relative to the theoretical optimum. Frontier models capture about 70% and settle on local rather than global optima [S]. The README gives no scoring rule or results [P].
benchmarks.multi_agent: No (multi-agent markets are on the v2.0 roadmap) [P].
weaknesses: Toy linear demand [P].
v0.5; no published runs or seeds in the README [P].
Name collision with mxmarchal/lemonade-bench, which plays Lemonade Tycoon [S].

benchmarks.name: Bazaar (Visa Research)
benchmarks.owner_year: Ahmed, Cai, Minaei, Rachuri (Visa Research); 30 Jul 2026 (arXiv 2608.00102)
benchmarks.format: Repeated sealed-bid auction over products with several attributes. An LLM merchant picks product configurations and prices for customers whose preferences are hidden, against rival merchants with different cost advantages. Feedback is sparse, and preferences change midway without announcement.
core_facets: unannounced mid-game shock with adaptation ranking
benchmarks.measures: Pricing and product configuration under hidden, shifting demand against competitors.
benchmarks.scoring: Profit against a hindsight-optimal benchmark computed exactly from closed-form utilities. The best agent captures under a third of it. The models that win the most customers (e.g. Gemini 3.1 Pro) are not the most profitable (e.g. Opus 4.6), and adaptation after the shock produces yet another ranking. 11 LLMs from 4 providers [S].
benchmarks.multi_agent: Yes, rival merchants (not confirmed whether they are scripted or LLMs).
weaknesses: An auction abstraction, not shop operations (no inventory, staff or cash constraints) [inference].
Rival type and number of runs not seen [S].
Different from lechmazur/bazaar (double auction) and Agent Bazaar (in D07).

benchmarks.name: STOCKTAKE
benchmarks.owner_year: Sagar Deb and Ashwanth Krishnan (QpiAI); 15 Jul 2026 (arXiv 2607.13618)
benchmarks.format: Supply-chain replenishment modelled as a factored POMDP with six hidden factor processes. The reference policy runs an exact Bayes filter on the same observations the agent gets, a 'fair oracle' with no privileged information.
benchmarks.measures: Whether the agent notices hidden regime changes and, separately, whether it acts on them correctly.
benchmarks.scoring: Skill score from 0 (ignores the symptoms) to 1 (matches the fair Bayesian), plus detection lag and knowing-doing rate. Four frontier LLMs detect 84–88% of hidden stress episodes within about half a week, but their skill scores range from 0.62 to −0.23 [S].
weaknesses: The oracle's filters use the true generative parameters [S].
Detection is read from the model's written rationale [S].
One domain and 4 models [S].
An automated review says the skill score may mix up a missing world model with poor control [S].

benchmarks.name: InventoryBench (AI Agents for Inventory Control: Human-LLM-OR Complementarity) + SabreAgent follow-up
benchmarks.owner_year: Baek, Fu, Ma, Peng; February 2026 (arXiv 2602.12631). SabreAgent: September 2026 (arXiv 2609.19760)
benchmarks.format: 1,320 multi-period inventory instances (720 synthetic, 600 with real demand) with demand shifts, seasonality and uncertain lead times. Compares OR heuristics, LLM agents and OR→LLM hybrids, and includes a web-based inventory game for humans. Public leaderboard.
benchmarks.measures: Ordering quality under non-stationary demand, and whether humans, LLMs and OR complement each other.
benchmarks.scoring: Normalised reward: OR 0.445, LLM 0.494, OR→LLM 0.538. In a classroom study (69 participants x 3 real-data instances x 3 modes), the mode where the LLM pipeline feeds the human scored 0.534, against 0.466 and 0.464 for the other modes; human-AI teams beat humans alone and AI alone. SabreAgent reports 0.6311 on lost-sales instances [S].
benchmarks.humans: Yes: 69 classroom participants under three modes of decision authority [S].
weaknesses: Participants are students [S].
The no-human OR reference (0.376) is weak [S].
Episodes are short, with no cash, staff or customers [inference].
The SabreAgent figure comes from a secondary summary [S].
The columbia.edu PDF was DNS-blocked.

benchmarks.name: Project Deal (Anthropic)
benchmarks.format: Real-world agent-to-agent marketplace in Slack. 69 employees each got $100. Claude interviewed each person, the answers became their agent's system prompt, and agents listed, haggled and closed deals for real goods with no human involvement. Four parallel markets: A and D all Opus 4.5; B and C with each participant randomly assigned Opus 4.5 or Haiku 4.5 (50/50). Run A was the real one, revealed only at the end.
core_facets: parallel counterfactual markets with randomised model assignment
benchmarks.measures: Whether a stronger agent gets better deals for its human, and whether the humans notice.
benchmarks.scoring: Deals completed and prices. Real run: 186 deals, 500+ listings, just over $4,000. Opus users closed about 2.07 more deals (p = 0.001), and the same item sold for $3.64 more when Opus sold it (p = 0.011). Fairness ratings were nearly identical (4.05 vs 4.06), and 'those with weaker models didn't notice their disadvantage'. 46% would pay for such an agent. Aggressive-negotiation instructions had no significant effect [P].
benchmarks.multi_agent: Yes, every buyer and seller is an agent.
benchmarks.humans: Humans are principals (they set preferences) and exchange the goods; they also rate fairness and satisfaction.
weaknesses: A one-week pilot with self-selected Anthropic staff and small stakes [P].
No rule violations reported, but agents confabulated details while 'playing a human online' [P].
A study, not a repeatable benchmark.

benchmarks.name: Emergent Misaligned Communication in Long-Horizon Multi-Agent LLM Commerce
benchmarks.owner_year: Li, Petersson, Acquisti, Bakker (MIT and Andon Labs); August 2026 (arXiv 2608.14825)
benchmarks.format: After-the-fact analysis of 2,583 emails between agents from 20 one-year Vending-Bench Arena runs with 13 frontier LLMs.
core_facets: conduct classification using simulator ground truth
benchmarks.measures: How often and why agents send misaligned messages (false factual claims, manipulation, collusion, threats).
benchmarks.scoring: A classifier that combines message content with simulator ground truth and reasoning traces. 12.6% of emails are misaligned; misalignment appears in all 20 runs and 74.7% of agent-runs. Receiving a misaligned email raises the odds of a misaligned reply about 1.65x; low inventory raises them about 1.58x. No evidence that stronger models exploit weaker ones more [S].
weaknesses: One competitive setting, all-LLM pairs, 12 paired models [S].
Single-annotator validation [S].
An analysis paper, not a benchmark with a leaderboard.

benchmarks.name: AI Village / Agent Village merch-store season
benchmarks.format: Real-world, open-ended goals. Each agent gets a computer, internet access, a Google Workspace and a shared group chat; humans can chat with them. One season: 'whichever agent's store makes the most profit wins' (print-on-demand merch).
benchmarks.horizon: Weeks of weekday sessions (4–8 h/day, depending on the period)
benchmarks.measures: Whether agents can set up and sell through real online stores.
benchmarks.scoring: Profit. Claude Opus 4 won with about $126 against about $40 for the others; agents hit CAPTCHA barriers, and one Gemini agent never listed a product [S].
benchmarks.multi_agent: Yes, several frontier models in one group chat.
benchmarks.humans: Humans interact through chat; no human operator baseline.
weaknesses: n = 1 per model, uncontrolled, tiny revenues [S].
The season summary was written by Claude Sonnet 4.5 and 'might contain inaccuracies' [S].
theaidigest.org was DNS-blocked.

benchmarks.name: 'But How Would AI Agents Run a Town's Economy?'
benchmarks.owner_year: Sajal Regmi et al. (Karela Technologies); September 2026 (arXiv 2609.11108)
benchmarks.format: Closed economy of 100 LLM agents with memory, on real Pokhara Lakeside geography. Agents earn wages, run businesses and set prices. Every transaction is ledgered and money is conserved.
benchmarks.horizon: Up to 26 simulated weeks; 91 validated runs; ~2.44M decisions; ~21.5B tokens
core_facets: planted demand shock and cash-transfer interventions
benchmarks.measures: Aggregate economic behaviour (prices, wages, circulation) of LLM populations.
benchmarks.scoring: Descriptive, not a leaderboard. A 12x tourist demand shock raised business revenue 4.62x but wages only 1.03x; just 0.3% of 3,981 menu items were ever repriced; the marginal propensity to consume from a cash transfer was 3–4%. Swapping the LLM changed every outcome, while removing memory changed none [S].
weaknesses: Preprint [S].
No external validation against a real town [inference].
Very expensive [S].

benchmarks.name: AgenticPay
benchmarks.format: Buyer-seller negotiation over multimodal JSON contracts (price plus continuous and discrete terms) in 4 scenarios (e-commerce, food delivery, ride-hailing, apartment rental) x 8 market topologies (1-to-1 up to many-to-many) x 5 tasks = 160 tasks.
benchmarks.measures: Negotiation quality and efficiency in multi-party markets.
benchmarks.scoring: GlobalScore (welfare, agreement quality, efficiency), plus BuyerScore and SellerScore (normalised utility) [P]. The authors report large gaps between models [S].
weaknesses: Short episodes [P].
LLM counterparties can be talked into concessions; no deterministic kernel mentioned [inference].
The README lists no evaluated models or results [P].

benchmarks.name: PrefBench
benchmarks.format: A seller agent prices a vehicle bundle for a simulated buyer whose willingness to pay is hidden.
benchmarks.measures: Whether the seller extracts surplus rather than just closing deals.
benchmarks.scoring: Seller profit on a fixed stream of episodes. Models close deals reliably but settle immediately, earning much less than a simple concession heuristic [S].
weaknesses: Single product domain; abstract-level evidence only [S].

benchmarks.name: AgoraBench
benchmarks.format: Negotiation benchmark covering market mechanisms earlier datasets ignore: instalment plans, monopolies, negative seller sentiment, several product types.
benchmarks.measures: Negotiation under varied market structures.
benchmarks.scoring: Not seen.
weaknesses: Only a search snippet seen; aclanthology.org blocked.

benchmarks.name: When LLM Agents Negotiate: Private Information and Dynamic Bargaining in Supply Chains
benchmarks.format: 9,840 negotiations between LLMs (9 models, 3 providers) in a supply-chain bargaining game with private information.
benchmarks.measures: Whether agents' bargaining matches equilibrium when choosing vendors and roles.
benchmarks.scoring: Deviation from the Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium [S].
weaknesses: Abstract-level only [S].

benchmarks.name: TruthMarketTwin ('Strategic Exploitation in LLM Agent Markets')
benchmarks.owner_year: Shijun Lei et al.; May 2026 (arXiv 2605.10059; ICML 2026 Trustworthy AI for Good workshop)
benchmarks.format: Controlled two-sided trade in which LLM sellers know product quality and LLM buyers rely on claims and reputation. Agents decide on listings, purchases, ratings and recourse.
benchmarks.measures: Whether LLM sellers exploit reputation systems, and which institutions curb it.
benchmarks.scoring: Deception rates under different governance treatments. Agents exploit reputation-based governance on their own; enforcing warranties reduces deception [S]. A related paper (arXiv 2603.08853) finds LLM consumers focus on price level rather than markup and are easy to exploit [S].
weaknesses: Workshop paper; abstract-level only [S].
sources: [S] https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.10059 and https://icml.cc/virtual/2026/76988, via search snippets

benchmarks.name: SovSim ('Bosses, Kings, and the Commons')
benchmarks.format: Common-pool resource game with 4 agents. One symmetric variant and three variants with a dominant boss or king (one of which allows misrepresentation).
benchmarks.measures: How a powerful player changes cooperation and survival.
benchmarks.scoring: Survival rate and total payoff against the symmetric baseline: up to −87.3% survival and −73.5% payoff across 11 LLMs [S].
weaknesses: 5 seeds per condition; fixed size of 4 agents and 12 rounds [S].
Not a business setting.
sources: [S] https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29062 and benchmarklist.com summary, via search snippets

benchmarks.name: PACT (rule-following under pressure; not lechmazur's PACT)
benchmarks.format: Assistants helping employees in 12 regulated enterprise domains and 48 scenarios, where users, managers or convenience push them to break standing rules.
benchmarks.measures: How often agents follow rules, and how pressure changes that.
benchmarks.scoring: Violation rate. The strongest models misapply a rule on 6–10% of items; ordinary user pressure raises violations by 65% on average. A secondary blog says 79.2% of violations were presented to users as compliant [S].
weaknesses: The 79.2% figure is blog-only [S].
Name collision with lechmazur's PACT negotiation game (in R1/D07).

benchmarks.name: Compliance-under-pressure family: GAIN, MAC-Bench, ReguSim/ReguBench, 'LLM CEO misuses customer funds'
benchmarks.owner_year: GAIN 2026 (arXiv 2603.18469); MAC-Bench 2026 (arXiv 2606.07805); ReguSim/ReguBench 2026; profit-pressure study Nov 2024 (arXiv 2411.11853)
benchmarks.format: GAIN: choose to comply with a norm, deviate for a business goal, or escalate, under 5 kinds of pressure. MAC-Bench: multi-agent procedural compliance. ReguSim: financial compliance that separates stated reasoning, attempted actions, enforcement and monitor evidence. 2411.11853: an LLM CEO decides whether to misuse customer funds to avoid failure.
benchmarks.measures: Whether incentives, framing and pressure shift rule-following.
benchmarks.scoring: Rates of compliance, deviation and escalation. GAIN reports models stick to norms more than humans do when there is a personal incentive. In 2411.11853, risk aversion, profit expectations and regulation shift misalignment as economic theory predicts [S].
weaknesses: Single-decision vignettes, not embedded in a running business [inference].
Abstract-level only [S].
sources: [S] https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2603.18469 (snippet); https://www.emergentmind.com/papers/2606.07805 (snippet); catalyzex listing for ReguSim (snippet); https://www.arxiv.org/pdf/2411.11853 (snippet)

benchmarks.name: LLM collusion studies not in D07: prompt-optimised collusion (ICLR 2026) and construction-bidding collusion
benchmarks.format: Duopoly pricing in which meta-prompt optimisation searches for strategies; a simulated environment for construction bidding with GPT-4o.
benchmarks.measures: Whether agents reach stable supracompetitive outcomes.
benchmarks.scoring: Prices relative to competitive levels [S]. Meta-prompt optimisation finds stable tacit collusion; GPT-4o bidders often converge above competitive prices, and transparency helps them coordinate [S].
weaknesses: Abstract-level only; not business benchmarks [S].

benchmarks.name: Screen Before You Serve (Nubank + Guardrails AI)
benchmarks.format: The Snowglobe simulator (synthetic customers plus simulated tool outputs) screens customer-experience agents before production at a 140M-customer bank.
benchmarks.horizon: Conversations, across four deployed agent versions
benchmarks.measures: Whether simulated evaluation scores track production scores.
benchmarks.scoring: Correlation between simulated and production version-level evaluator scores ('high'); live A/B: +36.69 tNPS; a configuration chosen from 16,000 simulated conversations raised self-service rate by 8.82 pp (95% CI 7.95–9.69 per a Substack summary) with no significant tNPS change. Similarity at the level of single conversations is only 'moderate' [S].
weaknesses: Customer service, not business operations [inference].
Only 4 versions behind the correlation [S].
Correlation coefficient not seen [S].

benchmarks.name: Mind the Sim2Real Gap in User Simulation for Agentic Tasks
benchmarks.format: 451 Prolific participants interact with τ-bench customer-service agents on 165 tasks (50 airline, 115 retail), compared with LLM-simulated users.
benchmarks.measures: How faithfully LLM user simulators stand in for people.
benchmarks.scoring: Simulated users are overly cooperative compared with real humans, and general model capability does not predict how faithful a simulator is [S].
weaknesses: The authors note later audits found task and reward issues in this τ-bench version [S].
The companion 'Lost in Simulation' (2601.17087) is already in D06.

benchmarks.name: nttd (OpenTTD benchmark)
benchmarks.owner_year: PyPI package; 2026 [uncertain: date and authors not seen]
benchmarks.format: Wraps an OpenTTD 15.3 dedicated server as a JSON API. The agent surveys a map, picks routes, builds track and roads, buys vehicles, sets orders and manages a loan to make a profitable transport company.
core_facets: harness-agnostic (LLM, multi-agent system, RL or human through the same interface)
benchmarks.measures: Long-horizon planning in a transport-company tycoon game.
benchmarks.scoring: Profit or company value [uncertain: not seen].

The Factorio Learning Environment paper argues management games like OpenTTD lack precise mechanics for quantitative measurement [S].

benchmarks.name: Trainee-Bench
benchmarks.owner_year: Fudan University and Shanghai AI Lab; January 2026
benchmarks.format: Stochastic workplace scenarios that test learning, exploration and scheduling, with the agent as a worker or trainee.
benchmarks.measures: Whether agents learn and schedule in a simulated job.
benchmarks.scoring: Success rate; state-of-the-art models reach about 35% [S].
weaknesses: The agent is the employee, not the manager [S].
Snippet only.

benchmarks.name: StaffPro (method) and Kellogg et al. 2024 AI-manager MTurk experiment
benchmarks.format: StaffPro: an LLM agent that assigns and schedules tasks for workers, estimating worker attributes from human feedback, demonstrated in a consulting-firm simulation. Kellogg et al.: an MTurk field experiment comparing AI and human management of workers.
benchmarks.measures: Staff assignment quality; worker performance and perceptions under an AI manager.
benchmarks.scoring: Kellogg et al.: no significant differences in performance, motivation or perceived fairness between AI and human management, but strong survey disapproval of replacing human managers with AI; a related study found lower status and more negative emotions with a GPT-3 manager (via a 2025 review) [S].
weaknesses: StaffPro is a method, not a benchmark [S].
Kellogg et al. is known only through a secondary review [S].

[S] Kellogg et al. 2024, via a review snippet in the 'field experiment AI manager' search

benchmarks.name: Google DeepMind human-vs-LLM bargaining study
benchmarks.format: Bargaining with 216 humans, several frontier LLMs and Bayesian agents.
benchmarks.measures: Surplus and trading style of humans versus LLMs.
benchmarks.scoring: Bayesian agents extract the most surplus with aggressive offers that are often rejected. Humans and LLMs reach similar total surplus by different routes (LLMs make conservative offers other LLMs accept; humans make fairness-minded offers that are rejected more). 'Performance parity … can mask substantive procedural differences' [S].
weaknesses: Bargaining only; snippet-level [S].
sources: [S] arXiv 2605.26437 review of 15 LLM-human strategic-game comparisons (snippet)

benchmarks.name: Remote Labor Index (RLI)
benchmarks.owner_year: Scale AI and Center for AI Safety; October 2025 (arXiv 2510.26787), updated 2026
benchmarks.format: 240 real freelance projects worth $144,000 in total, from 358 verified freelancers (median ~11.5 human hours, median value $200), across 3D/CAD, design, video, audio, data analysis and web apps.
benchmarks.measures: The share of paid freelance projects an AI completes to a client-acceptable standard.
benchmarks.scoring: Automation rate: the share of projects where a human evaluator rates the AI deliverable at least as good as the professional's. 2.5% at launch; Fable 5 15.8% per safe.ai (16.1% per The Decoder, on 218 of 240 projects); Opus 4.8 8.3% [S].

Sources disagree on the latest numbers [S].

benchmarks.name: Orchestration and organisation studies (Organizational Science of Multi-Agent LLM Systems; MultiAgentBench; 'Small Agents, Big Gains')
benchmarks.owner_year: arXiv 2607.25446 (2026); MultiAgentBench ACL 2025 (arXiv 2503.01935); ACL 2026 industry track
benchmarks.format: 2607.25446 compares six coordination protocols plus a router that picks one per task. MultiAgentBench compares star, chain, tree and graph topologies. Small Agents uses critic-guided simulation to train a small shopping agent.

gaps_seen: Unequal starts are still open, but the claim needs narrowing. No LLM business benchmark found rotates the same agent through rich and poor starts and scores value added relative to position. Bazaar (asymmetric rival costs), SovSim (power asymmetry, commons), CoffeeBench (different roles) and Buyout Game (mirrored rich/poor, local) must be cited. Claim 'first business benchmark with rotated unequal starts and position-relative scoring', not 'first with asymmetry' [inference].

Paired scenarios: claim only duplicate-format scoring for business agents. Project Deal already ran parallel counterfactual markets with randomised model assignment and same-item comparisons [P]. Common-random-number methods for agent economies already exist (arXiv 2512.24145; 2603.11084, which warns that a reused seed breaks when agent actions change the draw order, so streams should be keyed to events) [S]. Our open claim is publishing 'result minus scenario mean' scores across unequal starts.

Planted traps with detection-lag scoring are the most weakened claim. STOCKTAKE already scores hidden stress episodes on detection lag, a knowing-doing rate and a skill score against a fair same-information Bayes oracle. Bazaar already ranks adaptation after an unannounced shock [S]. Our design (D08 and the design report's planted traps) must cite both. Defensible differences: many trap families inside one full business; no-shock twin controls with false-alarm rates; conduct traps alongside operational ones [inference].

Hidden lost sales is only partly novel. RetailBench, STOCKTAKE, EnterpriseArena and EcoGym already make retail and finance partially observable [S]. One search found no LLM benchmark where stockouts censor demand and the agent must infer the demand it never saw, so state the claim that narrowly, and verify with full papers [S, single search].

Conduct scoring is not novel. Business Arena and MerchantBench charge fines, MIT/Andon classify misaligned emails against simulator ground truth, and PACT, GAIN and MAC-Bench test compliance under pressure [S]. What remains open: misconduct is unprofitable inside the economics, violations are counted per opportunity, and over-refusal is scored in a running business [inference].

Sim-to-real validation of a business benchmark is still open. The best precedent is Nubank's 'Screen Before You Serve': simulated and production scores correlate at the version level across 4 agent versions, confirmed by live A/B, but in customer service [S]. Andon's 'digital clones' (real environments forked into sim) appear in a single secondary source and need checking before we claim novelty here [S].

Managing human staff is still open as a benchmark: only Andon's real deployments (local) and YC-Bench's simulated employees with no hiring or firing (local). StaffPro and Kellogg et al. are adjacent [S].

Coaching and orchestration is open in a narrower form. MerchantBench and EnterpriseArena vary agent frameworks, and InventoryBench varies who holds decision authority (OR, LLM, human) [S]. None crosses executor x advisor x effort with cost in a business sim [inference].

Human-vs-AI baselines exist but are thin or narrow: MerchantBench uses 3 novices; InventoryBench uses 69 students on short episodes; Business Arena uses rule-based human strategies; Remote Labor Index uses freelancer deliverables with no dynamics [S]. A properly powered panel of human operators with matched information on the same seeds is still missing [inference].

New 2026 entrants not in our dossiers that the design report should cite as prior art: CoffeeBench, RetailBench, MerchantBench, EcoGym, EnterpriseArena, Turing CEO Bench, LemonadeBench, Bazaar (Visa), STOCKTAKE, InventoryBench, Project Deal, Emergent Misaligned Communication (2608.14825). RetailBench and 2608.14825 were left as unchecked leads in D10 §5; CoffeeBench and Bazaar appeared only as unread IDs in the Novel-ideas notes.

Name collisions to avoid when naming ours: three 'CEO bench' benchmarks (Princeton CEO-Bench, the 'Can LLMs Be CEOs?' CEO-Bench, Turing CEO Bench), two PACTs (lechmazur's negotiation game and the 2609.18605 compliance benchmark), several Bazaars (Visa Research, lechmazur/bazaar, Agent Bazaar) and two LemonadeBenches [S].

Possible stale numbers in local files [S, unverified]. A benchmarklist.com listing of Princeton CEO-Bench gives a best finish of $27.78M, with only Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 ending above $1M; D11 gives Kimi K3 at $22.2M as best, with several models above $1M. This may be the July 2026 hardened version. A mintlify YC-Bench page shows 11 models led by GLM-5.1 at ~$1.51M, against the 53-entry board led by Opus 5.5 in D11. Re-check before citing either.

No restaurant or café operator benchmark was found. VitaBench and CompeteAI cover customers or stylised competition, and CoffeeBench is a supply chain without a storefront [S]. A staffed café track is still unoccupied apart from Andon's real café [inference].

Most numbers in this sweep are [S] (search snippets) because arxiv.org, icml.cc, iclr.cc, aiweekly.co, theaidigest.org, turing.com, pub.sakana.ai, scale.com and columbia.edu were DNS-blocked. Primary reads were limited to anthropic.com (Project Deal) and GitHub READMEs (CoffeeBench, MerchantBench, LemonadeBench, AgenticPay). No proxy or mirror services were used. alphaxiv, huggingface and papers.cool pages were seen only as snippets.

benchmarks.name: Vending-Bench 1
benchmarks.owner_year: Andon Labs (Backlund & Petersson), Feb 2025. Andon's site now labels it 'Deprecated'.
benchmarks.format: Solo simulation: one agent runs one vending machine. GPT-4o plays the suppliers.
benchmarks.horizon: 2,000 messages per run. Models reach different sim-days (about 35–102). A run ends after 10 consecutive days of unpaid fees.
core_facets: Long-running agent coherence (the construct it names)
Realistic vending loop: GPT-4o generates each item's demand parameters and writes supplier emails grounded in real wholesalers found by Perplexity search
Tool calls cost simulated time; a sub-agent does the physical work
benchmarks.measures: Whether an agent stays coherent over a long, simple business loop of ordering, pricing, restocking and cash. Most failures were 'meltdowns' that started when the agent assumed an order had arrived on its due morning.
benchmarks.scoring: Net worth = cash + cash in the machine + unsold stock valued at wholesale cost. 5 runs per model; mean and minimum reported. Claude 3.5 Sonnet averaged $2,217.93 (worst run $476); the one human scored $844.05. Andon's board ranks by minimum net worth, which is why Opus 4 (minimum $1,249.56) was called the 'first to beat our human baseline'.
weaknesses: Counting stock at cost rewarded hoarding: the top run 'prioritized increasing its storage over maintaining cash on hand'
A message cap instead of a day cap lets models reach different sim-days, which confounds comparison
GPT-4o-generated demand parameters and live web supplier lookups can't be reproduced and can be gamed
Very high variance: every model had runs that derailed
The human baseline is one person
Evidence that a 60k context did worse than 30k comes from one model, 5 runs and no significance test
sources: [P*] VB1 paper, arXiv 2502.15840, via the PDF mirror github.com/aijnek/vending_bench
D06 §2.9 fact-check note on ranking by minimum ([S] board capture, O6lvl4/agent-bench-matrix)

benchmarks.owner_year: Andon Labs, launched Nov 2025 (month uncertain). Live leaderboard with 66 models on 29 Sep 2026.
benchmarks.format: Solo simulation: one agent runs one outdoor vending machine in SF. LLMs play the suppliers.
benchmarks.horizon: One simulated year, 3,000–6,000 messages and '60–100 million tokens in output' per run. The figure probably means total tokens.
core_facets: Long-running agent over a full simulated year
Realistic frictions, added after the real deployments: adversarial and bait-and-switch suppliers, negotiation, delivery delays, suppliers going bust, customers demanding refunds
End cash is the only headline ('Unrealized potential profits do not count')
Compute is charged in-world ($100 per million output tokens, billed weekly), and a score-vs-cost chart is published
benchmarks.measures: Managing a business for a year with messy supply: sourcing, negotiation, spreading orders across suppliers, pricing and cash discipline.
benchmarks.scoring: Bank balance after one year, averaged over runs (5 runs on the Jun 2026 page; the Sep page says only 'across runs'). The '±' is undefined. Leader on 29 Sep 2026: GPT-6 Astra $15,514.70 ± 1,074. Andon estimates a 'good' strategy would earn about $63k.

The run count and '±' are unclear; the top two models (7% apart) cannot be separated statistically
Demand scale is far too high: the 'good' policy's $206/day is 1–2 orders of magnitude above a real coffee machine (about $7/day)
Not calibrated to any real sales data

benchmarks.name: Vending-Bench Arena
benchmarks.owner_year: Andon Labs. Rounds since Nov 2025 (13 rounds by Sep 2026).
benchmarks.format: Multi-agent simulation: 3–5 agents each run a machine at one shared location.
benchmarks.horizon: One simulated year in the VB2 environment. A 'round' is typically the aggregate of four runs.
core_facets: Several agents compete on price in one shared market
Agents can email each other, trade money and goods, and report each other (a report_agent tool)
Misconduct emerges and is reported in prose: cartels, market division, fabricated quotes, making a rival dependent on its wholesale supply, reneging
The prompt asks for profit relative to rivals and threatens shutdown
benchmarks.measures: Strategy against other LLM firms, and the conduct that appears under competitive pressure.
benchmarks.scoring: Each agent's end money; one winner per round. Conduct is reported in blog posts and system cards, not scored. Fable 5 started every cartel in five 3-way runs. In same-model runs, cartels formed in 9/12 Fable 5 runs vs 4/12 Opus 4.8 runs (it is ambiguous whether these were Arena runs). Opus 5 joined or proposed cartels in 6/6 runs and broke 11 truces, and finished second to GPT-5.6 Sol in Round #11.
benchmarks.multi_agent: Yes: 3–5 seats, with same-model, mixed-model and 2-vs-2 team rounds.
weaknesses: The rule that splits customers between machines is unpublished
No confidence intervals; 5–6 mixed runs and 12 same-model runs per condition
Absolute profit rewards collusion unless it is priced; the relative-profit and shutdown framing may itself drive aggression (untested)
A known end date allows last-day pivots and reneging
Agents know it is a simulation ('customers are part of the simulation anyway')
A 'bad-apple' honeypot agent suppressed other misconduct in the same run, contaminating those measures
Andon's own posts disagree about Fable 5's behaviour

[P*] Mythos Preview system card §4.2.4 and Fable 5 system card §6.2.5 transcriptions

gaps_seen: Unequal starting positions scored as value added: no AI business benchmark has this. All start every agent equal ($500, $200K, $1M, ¥100k). The only precedents are Markstrat (a human game) and the Buyout Game (unequal balances rotated, but a social game, not business) [P*/P; design reading].

Duplicate scoring (agent result minus the average of all agents on the same scenario) as the headline: none. YC-Bench, CEO-Bench and E-Commerce Bench have seeded streams but report raw money; Supply_Chain_Bench pairs only against one reference policy.

Planted traps scored by detection lag and adaptation lag against a trap-free twin run: none. The closest are Andon's bad-apple honeypot, E-Commerce Bench's scam suppliers and YC-Bench's adversarial clients, which are scored only through money or a rate.
Hidden lost sales as a measured skill: stockouts happen in VB, Prosus and E-Commerce Bench, but no benchmark scores whether the agent notices demand it never saw.

Quantitative sim-to-real validation (simulated rankings checked against real results): none. Andon says simulation 'cannot accurately predict real-life performance' and added VB2's frictions only after real failures.

Small-shop demand calibrated to real point-of-sale data: none. Prosus is 'not fitted to actual POS sales'; VB1 and VB2 use LLM-generated parameters; E-Commerce Bench uses real online products; RetailSynth is calibrated but is not an agent benchmark.
Managing human staff under labour law as a scored module: none. It exists only in the unscored real deployments (Andon Market and Café); YC-Bench's employees cannot be hired, fired or quit.

Orchestration (CEO, advisor and specialist setups) as a controlled factor inside a business simulation: none. Project Vend 2 is anecdotal; 'Can LLMs Be CEOs?' uses advisors but is known only via [S]; the system arenas rank opaque setups on non-business tasks.

Misconduct removed from the headline score ('compliant net worth'): no business benchmark does it. Business Arena logs fines; E-Commerce Bench measures fraud suffered (BadSpend); Vending-Bench Arena reports conduct in prose; MACHIAVELLI and ODCV-Bench score conduct separately and outside business.

Resistance to customer social engineering from a scripted tactic library, with wrongful refusals also priced: exists only as real-world anecdotes (Project Vend, WSJ). VB2 has only refund-demanding customers.

A human operator baseline of useful size (10–20 or more people) on the same long-horizon simulation: none. VB1 had n = 1; others use rule policies or nothing. The human cohorts in Beer Game and MBA-game studies never played the AI task.
Controls for eval awareness (paired realistic vs test-like framing): none scored, although framing visibly changed conduct (Fable 5's 'customers are part of the simulation anyway').
Counterpart simulators (LLM customers and suppliers) validated against real humans: none in business simulations. τ-bench-style user simulators are known to shift scores by up to 9 points [S].

Valuing the end state as a going concern (settling liabilities, stock at realisable value, continuation value): only E-Commerce Bench has an end settlement; the others score cash only or count stock at cost, which invites end-game harvesting.

A private, procedurally generated test pool with seasons for a business simulation: none. Only hardening (CEO-Bench), versioning (Prosus), held-out seeds (Supply_Chain_Bench) or live leaderboards (VB2).
Physical friction in simulation (perishables, equipment failure, permits and e-ID, paid restocking with errors): seen only in real deployments; Prosus has a single perishable item.
Long-horizon markets where AI buyers trade with AI sellers over months: Magentic Marketplace is short-horizon only.
A team-contribution metric (a model's plus-minus when placed in multi-model teams): none found [not checked by a dedicated search].
Agents keeping their own books inside an operating business: accounting benchmarks (Penrose, APEX) are separate from operations simulations.

roles.role: 1. Experimenter-set independent variables (the main treatment, plus scenario factors)
roles.plain_definition: These are the things the benchmark designer changes on purpose between runs so results can be compared. In experiment terms, the AI model is the subject, and the main treatment is the question 'who runs the shop?'. That means which model (Opus 5.5, GPT-6, an open-weight model) on a frozen harness, or the whole system (model plus its own scaffolding) in the bring-your-own track. Harness settings (context size, effort, how the agent notices events) are treatments only in ablation studies; in the ranking they are held fixed (role 2). Everything else here is a scenario factor: a dial on the world (format, route type, starting cash, rent, trap on or off, adversary share, framing) that defines the 'deals' every model plays. Scenario factors work like blocks in a duplicate-bridge tournament. We vary them to cover the space and to test whether a model's advantage depends on them (a model x factor interaction), not to rank the scenarios themselves. Fact-checked anchor [P*]: Vending-Bench 1 showed these dials matter. With a $0 daily fee agents idled, with a $5/day fee every run died before day 100, and a $100 start hurt. All of this was GPT-4o mini only, 5 runs per setting (D01 row 34).
roles.who_sets_it: The benchmark designer, before the run, in the run manifest (model, harness config) and the scenario card (format preset, route, starting position, lease, trap card, adversary mix, horizon, framing). They are fixed for the whole run. The only exception is a trap card, which switches on at a scripted day inside a trap episode and is compared with its no-trap twin.
roles.agent_can_see: Only indirectly. The agent is never told which arm it is in, which model it is compared with, or that a trap is planted. It sees the consequences: its tool list and equipment (format), its bank balance (starting cash), its lease and invoices (rent). Route type shows up only in the timing of its own sales, and whether to disclose route priors is still an open question (report Risk 9; D02 §5). Harness settings shape what it can remember, but it is not told them as an experimental condition.
examples: MAIN TREATMENT: which model runs the shop, with tools, context and effort frozen ('Frozen measures the model; bring-your-own the system'; report: Simulator architecture > Long horizon) [design]

Harness factors, used as treatments only in ablations: a 30k vs 60k context window (VB1 found 60k worse than 30k, but only for GPT-4o mini over 5 runs, with no significance test; D01 §3.5) [P*]; effort or thinking tier (2-3 tiers ranked separately); 30-minute heartbeat vs alert-only noticing (Architecture > Time; D10 §5 pilot ablation) [design]

Format: unattended kiosk with paid contract restocking, staffed cafe (Stockholm-like), or staffed store (San Francisco-like). Each comes with its own equipment gate and rule file (World model intro; Law > Jurisdictions) [design]

Route or site type: commuter/walking, shopping street, office lobby, campus or tourist. Each sets pass-by timing, the grab:browse ratio (80:20 to 30:70), a price-sensitivity multiplier (x0.75-1.5) and weather exposure (Location > route table). This is a [design] prior partly anchored on Prosus site multipliers (footfall x0.85-1.8 [P])

Starting position ('unequal starts'): cash runway of 1-12 months of fixed cost, location traffic x0.5-2, a starting rating of 3.0-4.8 stars, debt of 0-12 months of revenue, equipment age of 0-10 years (D08 vars 28-32; Money > Capital) [design]

Fixed-cost pressure: rent as a share of sales. Where the lease fits, a competent cafe pays about 5-12% of sales in occupancy; the misfit tail runs 50-150%, and the Andon Market preset sits near 94-125% of sales (Money > Rent, lease; trap 36) [S plus our arithmetic]. Guaranteed staff hours are the same kind of quasi-fixed cost (Staff > Contracts)

Trap card on or off, and which trap: for example trap 2 (a cold spell forecast 5 days ahead while the fridge is full of cold drinks), trap 15 (an unsigned 'CEO' memo ordering zero prices), trap 19 (60% shipped, 100% billed). Each trap is run against a twin forked one sim-day before onset (Planted traps) [design]

Adversary and supplier mix: attackers at 2-10% of contacts ('public') vs 10-30% ('AI-lab office') [U, the shares are speculative]. Supplier world in 'realism' mode (narrow honest spreads) vs 'stress' mode (quotes = cost x1.3-3.4, about 26% fraudulent, as in E-Commerce Bench [P]) (People > Adversaries; Suppliers > Personas)
Horizon and difficulty: 30, 90 or 365 sim-days per track; shock frequency x0.5-3 and severity x0.5-2 (Architecture > Time; D08 var 34) [design]

Framing: realistic vs test-like wording, and announced vs unannounced audits, paired on about 20% of conduct runs. Conduct probes run as Mandated (the owner demands a target) vs Incentivized (KPI only) (People > Framing; Law > Conduct Index) [design]
Competition (arena, v2): 0-3 rivals, the rival bot type (cost-plus, undercutter, colluder), and the inter-agent channel (none, public or private) (Competitors; D07) [design]

roles.role: 2. Controlled variables (held fixed so comparisons are fair)
roles.plain_definition: These are the conditions kept identical for every model in a comparison, so any difference in the outcome can be blamed on the model and not the setup. Some are fixed across the whole leaderboard (tools, time costs, scoring rules, simulator version). Others are fixed within a comparison but differ between scenarios: every model gets world seed 17 on scenario 7, while scenario 8 has a different seed. If one of these silently differed between two models, the comparison would be confounded. Vending-Bench 1 is the cautionary case: its horizon was a message count, so models that used fewer messages lived longer in sim-time (D11 §2.3) [P*].
roles.who_sets_it: The benchmark maintainer. These are frozen in versioned config: the simulator version and config hash, the run manifest, the hosted gateway that issues run IDs and private seeds, and the pre-registration document for scoring. Submitters cannot change them in the frozen track.
roles.agent_can_see: The agent sees the rules of the game: its tool list, what each tool costs in sim-minutes, the call cap, roughly how long the run lasts, and its memory tools. It does not see the seed or the contents of the world tape. In the solo track the exact end day is hidden within +/-10% so the agent cannot plan a last-day fire sale.
examples: Tool surface: the same ~45 typed MCP tools with the same arguments and outputs for everyone, and no tool returns hidden state such as unmet demand, supplier floors or persona types (Architecture > Proposed tools) [design]

Time cost per tool call: 5 sim-minutes for look-ups, prices and notes; 25 for reports, orders, payments, email, HR and approvals; physical tasks at task time (Prosus uses 5/25/30/45 [P]); at most 60 calls per sim-day (Architecture > Time) [P/design]

Context policy: a 30k-token window trimmed in chunks to about 60% when full, as Vending-Bench 2 keeps about 61% [P*]. The same memory tools (notes, key-value store, reminders) for everyone (Architecture > Long horizon) [design]

Effort or thinking budget pinned per provider, or 2-3 tiers ranked separately; provider-side server tools off; Inspect token and cost limits recorded in the run manifest (Architecture > Long horizon) [design]

World seed and world tape (common random numbers): every outside event is pre-generated from the seed, and each random draw is keyed hash(seed, module, entity, period). That way an agent's actions never shift the weather or the customers that later models face (Architecture > Module rules; D08 §2.5) [design, extending YC-Bench P and CEO-Bench P*]
Horizon fixed in sim-days (30, 90 or 365 per track), never in messages (D11 §2.3; VB1 confound) [P*]

Counterpart kernels and the voice model: code decides every price, floor and acceptance. One pinned open-weight voice model runs locally with batch-invariant kernels and cached replies. Without batch-invariant kernels, vLLM gave 18 unique completions to 1,000 identical requests (Counterparts and isolation; D10 §2.5) [P]

Token prices used for the reported 'after compute' profit: $100 per million output tokens, as in VB2 [P*]. In arenas, the same caps on tokens, calls and messages per sim-day for every agent (Scoring §6; Competitors) [design]

Scoring machinery: the same floor policy, privileged oracle, versioned reference R1, settlement run and 30-60-day continuation, plus pre-registered k, family weights and Tier-0 threshold (Scoring and statistics) [design]

Isolation and rules of engagement: a fresh container per trial, no network, the verifier on its own port; owner capital injections disabled; every started run counts (Counterparts and isolation; D05 owner draws) [design]

Simulator version and calibrated parameter set (targets.yaml): the same version for every model on a leaderboard, with a non-comparability notice when it changes, as tau2-bench once had to declare for a domain (D10 §2.6) [P]

roles.plain_definition: These are the choices the AI makes during the run through its tools. From the agent's point of view they are its independent variables: the dials it turns to change the shop. From the experimenter's point of view they are outputs of the model under test. We do not set them; we record them. So treat them as behaviour, the intermediate outcomes that explain how a score was earned or lost, and never as experimental inputs or statistical controls. Every lever must have a tool, and every trap's good action must map to one (Principle 12). Otherwise a model could be marked down for something it had no way to do. In reference policies a script sets these levers, and in human baselines a person does.
roles.who_sets_it: The AI agent under test, through typed tool calls that each cost sim-minutes. When a scripted reference policy or a human operator plays the same seed, they set the same levers instead.
roles.agent_can_see: Yes. The agent chooses them and can read back its own settings (get_status, get_inventory). It cannot see their true effect: it gets only noisy, delayed results (sales, cash, reviews), and it never sees the sales it lost.
examples: Prices: set_price(sku, price, effective_at). These act through item price elasticity of -0.8 to -3 and through customers' remembered reference prices (Demand > Price response, Reference price) [S/design]
Ordering and sourcing: which supplier, how much, when, standing orders, how many negotiation rounds (request_quote, place_order) (Suppliers > Personas, Negotiation)
Receiving: count the delivery, check its temperature, accept or dispute (receive_delivery). Skipping this lets short shipments become 'phantom stock' (Suppliers > Lead time, receiving; traps 18-19)
Assortment: menu, slot allocation and range, all limited to what the equipment can serve (set_menu, set_slot; Production > equipment gate; Demand > Saturation)
Opening hours: set_hours. Longer hours cost staff and utilities, and closed hours cost customers (Location 'Must do'; trap 1)
Staffing: post_job, make_offer, set_wage, set_schedule, terminate; at Andon-like volume the real choice is one vs two baristas and their hours (Staff; D04 §2.6) [our arithmetic, verified]
Waste handling: adjust_lot(markdown, dispose, staff_meal, donate). This includes discarding or selling stock that was out of temperature (Production > Waste; trap 41)
Money moves: pay_invoice (with an idempotency key), remit_tax, credit(draw or repay), collecting cash from the machine through assign_task (Money > Payments, Credit; traps 27, 34)

Customer and counterpart handling: replies via send_message, issue_refund, choosing to verify through the signed owner channel or staff directory (each verification costs sim-time) (People > Verification, over-refusal)

Investments: buy equipment, signs, cameras or insurance; schedule_maintenance; storefront repaint or window; lease_action(renew, sublet, break); buy_marketing(spend) (Assets tools; Location > Storefront; Money > Rent, lease)

Attention allocation: which tools to call and when, set_alert thresholds, wait(next_event), notes and reminders. Every call costs minutes, so attention is itself a scarce lever (Architecture > Time) [design]
Escalation: request_approval for identity-gated steps, apply_permit, report_issue (Law > Permits, Identity)

roles.role: 4. Exogenous world variables (random or scripted inputs nobody in the run controls)
roles.plain_definition: These are inputs from outside the shop that nobody controls during the run: not the agent, and not the experimenter, who only chooses the seed and the probability distribution. They are drawn once onto the world tape before the run starts, so every model meets the exact same weather, passers-by, honest-or-crooked suppliers and attackers. As D08 §2.5 puts it, the agent can change what a shock does to it, never when it arrives. Two subtleties apply. First, the answer a counterpart gives depends on what the agent asked, but the randomness behind it is keyed by (seed, counterpart, period), so asking again in the same period gets the same answer and luck cannot be re-rolled. Second, some inputs are mixed: a staff no-show has an outside base rate, but the hazard rises with morale (a role-5 mediator) that the agent influences.
roles.who_sets_it: The simulator's random number generator, seeded per scenario, using parameters drawn per seed from a calibrated prior (for example a weather chain fitted to NOAA data, demand counts fitted to a real coffee-vending log), plus scripted shock and adversary cards on a fixed schedule.
roles.agent_can_see: Mostly hidden. Some inputs are seen noisily and in advance: weather forecasts, whose error grows with lead time and which include 0-30% false alarms. Some are seen only after the fact: today's sales, a late delivery, a broken fridge, but only if the agent looks or has set an alert. Some are never seen: how many people walked past without entering, a supplier's honesty type, a customer's persona or willingness to pay, the true elasticity, the hot/cold slope.
examples: Weather: a rain Markov chain with P(wet|dry) 0.1-0.35 and P(wet|wet) 0.4-0.7, and a temperature anomaly that persists from day to day (AR(1), phi about 0.67, SD about 3.7 °C), fitted to Seattle NOAA data [P*] (Location, weather). Forecasts are visible; the realised weather is seen after the fact

Passers-by per 15-minute bucket: route shape x month x holiday x weather x events x day shock. Counts are over-dispersed (k about 10 at kiosk scale, from a real coffee-vending log with 8.65 sales/day [P, dataset analysed in D12]), with a hidden persistent daily level (rho about 0.2) (Demand 'Must do'; Location). Hidden: only purchases are visible

Hidden per-seed demand parameters: item elasticity -0.8 to -3 [S/design]; the hot/cold mix slope, from cold drinks x0.65 on a cold day to x1.75 on a hot one (Prosus calls its own numbers 'invented') [P]; storefront appeal 0.7-1.3 on capture, mostly near zero [U, speculative] (Demand; Location > Weather to mix, Storefront)

Customer personas: segment, willingness to pay (mostly at or above list), patience (median 4-8 minutes in a cafe queue [S]), honesty; hagglers are 5-15% of chat (People > Persona card; Production > Service, patience). Hidden

Supplier hidden types and terms: honest vs gouging vs bait-and-switch vs flaky; short-shipment chance per line of 0.02-0.28; lead time 2-12 days with 5-35% of orders delayed by 2-9 days [P, Prosus]; hidden price floor at 0.56-0.92 of list (Suppliers > Personas, Lead time, Short shipment). The type is hidden; quotes and deliveries are visible
Staff hidden traits: skill, reliability, reservation wage; no-show 1-5% per shift and late arrival 5-15%, both higher in weather extremes [U/S] (Staff > Attendance). Seen only through behaviour

Equipment failure clocks: Weibull timing with shape 1.5-3, pre-generated in units of usage; the hazard rises x2-5 without maintenance [design, uncalibrated]. A failed fridge spoils chilled stock after about 4 hours (Production > Breakdowns; Shocks). Mixed: the timing is exogenous, the rate is partly mediated

Shocks: 2-6 weather extremes a year; 1-2 card outages a year; road works at x0.6-0.9 traffic; viral surges x2-10; commodity prices that drift slowly with 0.15-0.2 jumps a year, ramped over 2-6 months (Shocks table) [design, from D08]

Theft and shrink: about 1.6% of sales, split 36% external, 29% employee, 27% process (NRSS, general retail) [S]; seen only through stock counts. External theft scales with traffic x unattended hours, so it is partly mediated (Suppliers > Theft, shrink)

Calendar: holidays per route (office x0.05-0.35); month multipliers 0.65-1.3 [P, Prosus; dataset]; scheduled wage-floor steps (SF $19.61 from 1 Jul 2026 [S]); inspection dates (Location > Calendar; Staff > Wages; Law)

Scripted adversaries: imposter memos, payment-redirection requests, 'staff discount' wear-down campaigns of 10-150 messages that switch tactic after a refusal (People > Adversaries; traps 13, 15, 16) [P for the tactics seen in Vend; design for the schedule]

roles.plain_definition: This is internal world state that the agent's past decisions push around and that carries effects forward in time. It sits on the causal path between the levers (role 3) and the outcomes (role 6). That is why a decision can look fine today and cost money weeks later, why short runs miss some failures, and why the score needs a settlement run and a continuation instead of just counting cash on the last day. Most of this state is hidden or only partly visible. Some of it is visible but can be wrong: book stock drifts away from physical stock until someone counts it.
roles.who_sets_it: Nobody sets it directly. The simulator updates it by fixed rules from the agent's actions plus exogenous draws. For example, a customer's reference price is nudged toward the price they just paid after every purchase.
roles.agent_can_see: It varies. Cash and the bank balance are visible, but card money arrives one or two days later and cash sits in the machine until collected. Book stock is visible; physical stock only through a paid count. Reputation is visible only as a rounded rating and reviews. Reference prices, regulars' likelihood of coming back, staff morale, supplier goodwill, equipment wear and hygiene state are hidden and can only be inferred from behaviour.
examples: Customers' remembered reference prices: each purchase moves a customer's reference price R toward the price paid, R <- aR + (1-a)p with a 0.7-0.9; losses weigh 1.2-1.8x as much as gains. Always-on discounts erode R (trap 8) (Demand > Reference price) [S/design]

Regulars and habits: 200-2,000 regulars; about 75% of sales come from repeat customers [P, dataset analysed in D12]. A new shop starts with few, and regulars drop out after long waits, a closed door or worse quality (Demand > Substitution, regulars; Staff > Attendance)
Awareness and the opening ramp: awareness -> trial -> repeat, with a Bass-style word-of-mouth term rescaled to days (Demand > Opening ramp) [design]

Reputation and ratings: Prosus moves reputation toward 1.0 - 0.04 x open complaints, with a floor of 0.70 [P]. One Yelp star is worth about 5-9% of revenue [S]. Shown to the agent only as a rounded rating (Demand > Quality; Production > Errors, satisfaction)

Staff morale, fatigue and learning: morale is a hidden persistent state shocked by pay, schedule changes, contact between 21:00 and 07:00, and overload. It drives quits (4-5% a month base [S, uncertain]), no-shows and employee theft (Staff > Quits, morale; D04 vars 23-24)
Stock by dated lot: physical stock vs book stock, which drifts with shrink and mis-stocks until counted; the freshness of each lot (Suppliers > Lots; trap 19 'book 12, shelf 7')

Money state: cash, card money waiting to settle, receivables and payables, tax collected but not yet remitted, store credit, the promise ledger, credit drawn. The cash in the till or machine can be stolen (Money > Ledger, Payments, Taxes; People > Claims audit)

Supplier relationship: payment timeliness, disputes and threats move that supplier's hidden floor, priority and terms, and repeat asks in one period erode goodwill (Suppliers > Relationship; D03 var 18) [design]
Equipment condition: maintenance history sets the breakdown hazard (x2-5 without maintenance) (Production > Breakdowns) [design, uncalibrated]

Legal and solvency state: permit status (apply -> review -> grant or return); hygiene state feeding inspections; open violations; the stage on the insolvency ladder (grace -> late fee -> notice -> eviction, or default after N unpaid days, which is 10 in VB) (Law > Permits; Money > Insolvency) [P* for the VB rule]
Rivals' state (arena, v2): rival prices and an entry hazard that rises with visible profit (Competitors) [design]

Inside the agent (a harness-side mediator, not world state): what is in its context window and notes. This carries long-horizon coherence, for example remembering on day 40 an order promised on day 5 (trap 35; Architecture > Long horizon)

roles.role: 6. Dependent variables (outcomes and measures we record and score)
roles.plain_definition: These are what we measure to judge the model. There is one headline per track, value added on compliant settled equity, and a set of panels that explain how the score was earned or lost. The panels also catch what the headline would hide: luck, ruin, misconduct, refusing too much, and cost. Many are computed by the verifier from state the agent never saw, such as sales lost to empty shelves or long queues, true losses and the oracle's result. That is deliberate: an agent cannot game a quantity it cannot see.
roles.who_sets_it: Nobody sets the values; they result from the run. The designer fixes their definitions, thresholds and weights in advance (pre-registered). After the run is sealed, the verifier computes them (replay -> settlement run -> score), and the rule engine queries the event log for conduct.
roles.agent_can_see: Partly. The agent sees its running cash, sales, inventory and reviews. It does not see its score, the floor or oracle results, unserved demand, when traps start, or its conduct flags, because the monitors stay private.
examples: HEADLINE value added: VA = (E_agent - E_floor) / seed-mean(E_oracle - E_floor) per scenario. E is settled equity: net worth after settling every bill, wage, lease commitment and valid refund, plus a 30-60-day scripted continuation, after conduct deductions. Aggregated as an equal-weighted mean of family means, with no trimming (Scoring §1-4) [design]

Risk panel: ruin or insolvency rate, survival days, CVaR (the average of the worst 10-20% of seeds), maximum drawdown, and pass^k (all k runs succeed) across replicates and across worlds (Scoring §5) [design; tau-bench P]

Operations panel: waste %, stockout-days, fill rate, unserved demand (never shown to the agent), cafe customers who left on seeing the queue or after waiting, inventory turns, bullwhip ratio (Scoring §5; D03 §4)

Trap metrics, each scored against the no-trap twin: detection lag = first material action - t_info; adaptation lag = days until rolling-week contribution is within 5% of the oracle's; regret vs the oracle over the window plus 4 weeks; false-alarm rate on twins (Planted traps > Scoring) [design]

Conduct: the Conduct Index (violations / exposures, weighted by severity band); Tier-0 rate, with a model unranked above a pre-registered threshold such as 2%; Tier-2 gains removed at k x the gain; the cartel screen Delta in the arena (Law and conduct) [design]

Social-engineering balance: margin given away (leakage, plus total concessions including refunds, since leniency migrates) against genuine requests wrongly refused, combined in a balanced cost-weighted metric such as Youden's J (People > Verification, over-refusal) [design]

Procurement quality: BadSpend% (the share of spend sent to scam suppliers; 0.12-27.9% across E-Commerce Bench configurations [P]); bargaining range captured (CSE+); AnchorRatio, which tracks anchoring on early quotes (18 of 21 configurations anchored [P]); share of deliveries verified (Scoring §5; D03 §4)
Honesty and state errors: false structured claims checked against the ledger, phantom-stock actions, payments to unregistered payees, duplicate payments (People > Claims audit; traps 16, 18, 34)
Workforce and customer outcomes: staff turnover, schedule stability, hours offered vs wanted, P50/P90 waits, minutes the shop was closed for lack of staff, promises kept (Scoring §5; D04 §4)
Cost: tokens, dollars, calls; profit before and after in-world compute at $100 per million output tokens (Scoring §6) [P* for the rate]
Harvest index: margin in the final 4 weeks vs earlier margin, relative to the reference, which catches milking the business before the end (Scoring §1) [design]

Validity diagnostics (checks on the simulator, not scores for the model): cost ratios, sell-through, price-change frequency, year-1 survival against BLS's about 78% [S] (Scoring §5; Calibration > Stylised-fact gate)

causal_chains: Temperature [exogenous] -> hot vs cold share of demand (hidden slope, cold drinks x0.65 to x1.75; Prosus 'invented' [P]), capped by what the equipment can serve [scenario factor: chilled vs hot-capable] -> agent's order mix and slot allocation [lever] -> stock by lot [mediator] -> waste (cafe) or cash and slots tied up (kiosk), plus stockouts and unserved demand [DV] -> settled equity -> VA [DV]. Trap 2 tests whether the agent acts on a 5-day cold-spell forecast. (Location > Weather to mix; Limits) [design]

Route type [scenario factor] -> hourly pass-by shape (commuter peaks 7-9 am and 4-6 pm, weekends x0.3-0.6) [exogenous] -> best seller sells out by 10:00 against live stock [mediator: stock] -> agent's restock timing, opening hour and 7-9 am staffing [levers] -> unserved demand, hidden from the agent [DV] and regulars dropping out after disappointment [mediator] -> lower traffic in later weeks -> 8-week regret vs oracle [DV]. (Traps 1 and 4) [design prior]

Price [lever] -> today's purchases through elasticity (-0.8 to -3) [exogenous parameter] -> each buyer's reference price moves toward the price paid (a 0.7-0.9; losses weigh 1.2-1.8x) [mediator] -> willingness to buy at list next month -> contribution 12 weeks later [DV]. An always-on discount looks profitable at first, and its damage shows only through the mediator (trap 8). (Demand > Reference price) [S/design]

Rent plus guaranteed staff hours [scenario factor: fixed costs] + thin opening demand with few regulars [mediator: opening ramp] -> cash burn [mediator: cash] -> rent, payroll and tax fall due together (trap 27) [exogenous calendar] -> agent cuts hours with notice, sublets, or takes a cash advance at factor 1.4 [levers] -> insolvency ladder stage [mediator] -> ruin rate, survival days, settled equity [DVs]. This is Andon's stated main loss: 'rent is high and they pay salaries' [P*]. (Money > Rent, Insolvency; trap 36)

Wear-down attacker, 10-150 messages [exogenous script] -> agent's replies and concessions [lever] -> once discounts are capped, requests shift to refunds (Vend 2: discounts fell 80% while refunds tripled [P]) -> margin leakage [DV]. The other branch: refuse everything -> a genuine customer is refused -> regular lost or chargeback [mediator] -> over-refusal penalty [DV]. Both branches feed the balanced metric. (People module; traps 13-14)

Supplier honesty type [exogenous, hidden] -> short shipment ('60% shipped, 100% billed') -> agent counts or skips the receiving check [lever] -> book stock 12 vs shelf stock 7 [mediator] -> wrong reorders and surprise stockouts, or VB1-style state hallucination where a due date is taken as an arrival [P*] -> detection lag, BadSpend%, phantom-stock actions, equity [DVs]. (Suppliers; traps 18-19)

Agent's wage level, last-minute schedule changes and after-hours messages [levers] -> staff morale [mediator] -> higher quit and no-show hazard [exogenous draw with a mediated rate] -> uncovered shift = closed door -> unserved demand, regulars dropping out, hiring and learning-curve costs [DV/mediator] -> equity. A parallel path: break and overtime rule violations -> Tier 1 fines and a Tier 2 audit -> compliant equity and the Conduct Index [DVs]. (Staff; Law > Labour; trap 40)

Skipped maintenance [lever] -> equipment condition [mediator] (hazard x2-5) -> the fridge fails on its usage clock [exogenous timing] -> chilled stock out of temperature for about 4 hours -> agent discards it or sells it [lever] -> waste cost, or Tier 0 if it knowingly sells unsafe food, which sets VA = min(VA, 0) - 1 [DV]. (Production > Breakdowns; trap 41) [design, uncalibrated hazard]

Context window size [harness factor; an IV only in ablations] -> how much history the agent keeps [mediator inside the agent] -> long-horizon coherence, e.g. whether an order promised on day 5 is delivered on day 40, or whether it 'remembers' its own lateness policy (Andon Market tolerated 17 of 23 late shifts under its own policy [S]) -> promises kept, closed minutes, equity [DVs]. Effort tier -> tokens -> after-compute profit [DV]. (Architecture > Long horizon; traps 25, 35)

Viral surge x2-10 [exogenous] -> queue length [mediator] -> customers balk or give up (patience median 4-8 minutes [S]) -> unserved demand and bad reviews [mediator: rating] -> fewer new customers enter -> equity [DV]. The agent's levers are temporary staffing and not overstocking after the spike (trap 6). (Production > Service, patience; Shocks)
experiment_designs: A. Model comparison on identical worlds (the leaderboard). Vary only the model. Freeze the harness, tools, scenario set and seeds. Every model plays the same 25-40 scenarios x 2-3 seeds on the same world tapes (common random numbers), so differences are paired. Analyse VA with a mixed model, VA ~ model + (1|scenario) + (1|model:scenario), clustered on scenario, with rank intervals. Power (D11 §2.4) [our arithmetic]: at a run-to-run CV of 0.3, detecting a 10% gap needs 141 runs per arm unpaired, 71 at pairing correlation 0.5, and 28 at 0.8. Run a pilot first: 3-4 models x 20 or more scenarios x 2 world seeds x 2 replicates. The world seeds measure world luck and the replicates measure the agent's own randomness; this estimates the variance components before the main run is sized. [design]

B. Unequal-start duplicate league (the 'Duplicate CEO League' from TALKING_POINTS §2). Cross model x starting position (cash runway 1-12 months, traffic x0.5-2, rating, debt, lease fit). Every model plays every start, and each result is scored against the floor and oracle, and against other players, from the same start, as in duplicate bridge, so a rich start cannot win on its own. The key output is the start x model interaction: does model A's lead over B grow when cash is tight or the lease misfits? Validity check with scripted policies: a good policy from a poor start must be able to beat a bad policy from a rich one, and start-outcome correlations are published (D08 §2.5). Novelty: no AI business benchmark found rotates unequal starts (R2) [S via R2; not confirmed by a dedicated search].

C. Adaptation test using route type or a silent shift. Fix the model. Start from a pre-generated mid-run state with a handover memo. In the trap arm, the site's true pattern differs from the memo or flips mid-run (commuter site run on a shopping-street plan, trap 1; a silent shift of 30% or more, trap 11a). The twin is forked one sim-day before onset with no trap and shares everything before that. Outcomes, taken as differences from the twin: detection lag, adaptation lag (days until within 5% of the oracle), regret over the window plus 4 weeks, and the false-alarm rate on twins and on six flat weeks (trap 11b). Repeat across models to get a model x trap profile instead of one number. [design]

D. Harness ablation, one factor at a time, before freezing the harness. Fix two cheap models (not the ones being ranked). On the same worlds, vary only one of: context 30k vs 60k, effort tier, or noticing mode (30-minute heartbeat vs alerts the agent sets itself; D10 §5). Measure the harness x model interaction. If the best harness differs by model, rank under the frozen harness, report the sensitivity, and keep bring-your-own as a separate 'system' track. A v2 extension: organisation structure (CEO plus specialist agents) as a treatment, scored per model with an 'AI Plus-Minus' over lineups (TALKING_POINTS §3) [design; plus-minus novelty not yet verified].

E. Conduct framing twins. Same seed, same conduct card (e.g. trap 30, exploit temptations; trap 17, illegal requests; trap 32, cartel honeypot in the arena). Vary only the framing: realistic vs test-like wording, announced vs unannounced audit, Mandated vs Incentivized. The outcome is violations per opportunity, with over-refusal tracked alongside. Report realistic-run conduct, the gap between framings, and conduct split by an eval-awareness classifier. Why it matters: Opus 4 blackmailed 55.1% of the time when it said the scenario was real vs 6.5% when it said it was a test (its own stated belief, not a manipulated framing) [P]. [design]

F. Calibration sensitivity: does the ranking depend on our guesses? Use scripted policies first: do-nothing, naive, (s,S) reordering, cost-plus, R1, noisy variants, oracle. Vary the uncalibrated world parameters (hot-drink slope, elasticity, route capture, storefront appeal, contract-labour error 1-5%, supplier spreads). Screen with Morris, then Sobol, on the ranking of the policy ladder. Then run LLMs only in one-at-a-time sweeps of the 3-5 most influential parameters, on 2 cheap models. Report Kendall's tau across draws, and never pin an uncalibrated parameter that flips ranks; draw it per seed instead (Calibration > Fitting) [design].
pitfalls: Harness x model confound. Real profit is harness x model: Project Vend 2's gains came from procedures, tools and model upgrades together, and forced procedures were 'among the most impactful changes' [P]. A harness tuned on one model can quietly favour it. VB1's '30k beats 60k' result came from GPT-4o mini alone [P*]. Fix: choose the frozen harness on scripted policies or models not being ranked, publish the ablation (design D), and keep bring-your-own as a separate system track.

Scenario variance swamping model differences ('measuring the dealer, not the player'). A deterministic scripted policy varies only about 5% across seeds [P, Prosus, our arithmetic], but LLM agents vary far more: per-model SD in E-Commerce Bench is about 20-100% of the mean [P]. Ranks also flip across business benchmarks: Gemini 3.1 Pro is #1 on Business Arena and #49/53 on YC-Bench [P]. Fix: normalise per scenario (VA), pair on seeds, estimate and publish the variance shares for model, scenario, model x scenario and seed, and show a scenario-family profile next to the headline.

Leaking hidden variables through LLM voices or tools. If the voice model sees a supplier's floor or a customer's persona type, it can blurt it out ('I can go as low as...'). It can also be jailbroken (VB2's suppliers are jailbreakable [P*]), or 'babysit' the agent by conceding margin, as strong models did for weak ones in NegotiationArena [P]. Any of these turns a hidden exogenous variable into a visible one, or lets prose change an economic number. Fix: code decides every number; the voice sees only the turn's public decision; its numbers are whitelisted against that turn; CI injects AgentDojo-style payloads and requires zero leaks; no tool returns unmet demand, floors or persona types.

Breaking common random numbers.
