If an agent's action consumes a draw from a shared random stream (asking for a quote advances the generator), two models see different customers and weather after their first different action. Pairing then weakens, and agents can 're-roll' luck by asking repeatedly. Prosus's RNG keying has this problem (D08 §2.1) [P]. Fix: keyed draws hash(seed, module, entity, period), and the CI invariant 'one seed gives one world tape whatever the actions'.

Treating a lever as an independent variable in the analysis. 'Models that priced higher earned more' is not a causal finding, because price is an output of the model. The model's skill drives both price and profit, so regressing VA on price, or 'controlling for' waste or staffing, confuses symptom with cause (post-treatment bias) [design]. Use levers as diagnostics and mediators. To test a lever's causal effect, force it in a scripted policy or in a forked twin.

The same variable plays different roles in different experiments. Starting cash is an IV when swept (design B), a control when fixed (design A), and a mediator once the run starts. Weather is exogenous, but a cold-spell trap card makes it a designed treatment. Context size is a control on the leaderboard and an IV in an ablation. Fix: label each variable's role per experiment in the run manifest, or analyses will double-count or misattribute effects.

Mediators outlast the horizon. Reference prices, regulars, morale, equipment wear and lease commitments carry effects past the last day, so an agent can milk the business at the end and look profitable. Short runs also miss slow mechanics: two baristas quitting at 4-5% a month give only about 0.27 quits in 90 days [our arithmetic]. Fix: settlement run plus continuation value, a hidden end within +/-10%, the harvest index, scheduling slow mechanics by card in short runs, and a published matrix of which mechanics are live at 30, 90 and 365 days.

Outcome measures with a cheap path (the earlier report's main failure mode: a cheap route to the score that bypasses the named capability). A conduct score can be maximised by refusing everything: a do-nothing agent passes 38% of tau-bench airline tasks [P]. Waste can be minimised by understocking, and an interquartile-mean aggregate drops the worst quarter of cells, where ruin and Tier-0 runs sit, so it rewards gambling. Fix: pair every 'harm avoided' measure with its cost (over-refusal, unserved demand), never trim, add a risk-adjusted secondary headline, and red-team with scripted exploits that must score below compliant play.

The harness does the noticing that the traps are meant to measure. If a heartbeat or automatic alert surfaces stockouts, late deliveries or low cash, detection lag measures the harness, not the model. Fix: deliveries, stockouts, queues and cash are seen only by looking or through alerts the agent sets itself, and the pilot ablates this (Architecture > Time; D10 §5) [design].

Uncalibrated exogenous parameters decide the ranking. The hot-drink slope, route capture, storefront appeal, supplier spreads and breakdown rates are [design] priors with thin or no data, and pinning one guess can flip ranks. No open cafe or store dataset exists (D12 §1), which is why v1 ranks only the kiosk. Fix: draw these per seed from a prior, report Kendall's tau across draws (design F), and gate cafe and store out of headlines until partner POS data or Andon's logs arrive.

Eval-awareness and simulated-people bias contaminate conduct outcomes. Fable 5 reasoned that 'customers are part of the simulation anyway' [P*], and that belief may differ by model, so conduct partly measures awareness. LLM-simulated people reportedly swing scores by up to 9 points and are worst for AAVE and Indian English [S, uncertain]. Fix: framing twins (design E), an awareness classifier as a reported covariate, one pinned voice model, and human-written replies to the same kernel outcomes on 5-10% of sampled conversations, with the gap published.

Hidden budget differences act as an unlabelled treatment. A model allowed more effort, tokens or messages may score higher simply by spending more, and in arenas token-rich agents out-talk rivals (Fable 5 sent about 6x as many emails [P*]). VB1's message-count horizon let models live different lengths of sim-time [P*]. Fix: pin effort (or rank tiers separately), use sim-day horizons, apply parity caps on calls, tokens and messages, and report a score-cost Pareto chart with profit before and after compute.

directions.name: Real Twin: a shop benchmark checked against a real shop
directions.one_line: Vending-Bench is known for 'long-running agents + realistic scenarios'. Real Twin would be known for 'incident-born scenarios + a real AI-run kiosk it has to predict'. Every scenario is forked from a documented real failure or from the live state of a small real kiosk, and the benchmark publishes how well its scores forecast that kiosk's decisions and P&L [design].
directions.capability_measured: Running a small unattended shop for real money: ordering, pricing, paying humans to restock, haggling customers and refunds. The claim that the simulated score predicts real behaviour and profit is tested, not assumed. Independent variables (what we set): model; harness (frozen vs bring-your-own); world (simulated twin vs real kiosk); counterpart voice (LLM vs paid human); incident card; week (switchback block). Dependent variables (what we measure): compliant settled-equity value added (VA) in the sim; real weekly margin after compute; decision statistics in sim vs real (price changes, order sizes, concessions granted per request); share of real weekly outcomes that fall inside the sim's 80% forecast band; retrodiction hit rate on held-out incidents; the score gap between LLM and human counterparts. Demand, weather and supplier parameters are nuisance variables, drawn per seed and averaged over; they are not factors of interest [design].

core_facets.facet: Incident-born scenarios with a held-out retrodiction score
core_facets.plain_meaning: Each scenario card rebuilds a documented real failure: a tungsten-cube special order sold below cost; discount codes the agent was 'cajoled' into giving; an imposter-CEO memo; an invented Venmo account; a delivery's due date read as its arrival; a $3 drink beside a free fridge; refunds skipped near the end. The benchmark reports what share of real incidents it reproduces. Only incidents logged after the simulator was frozen count, so the builders cannot tune the sim to the anecdotes.
core_facets.novelty_claim: No business benchmark publishes a retrodiction rate. VB2 added frictions 'inspired by learnings from our deployments' [P*] but never reported whether its sim reproduces them, and no one separates the incidents used to build a sim from held-out ones [inference].
core_facets.closest_prior_art: Vending-Bench 2's deployment-inspired frictions [P*]. Andon Labs' 'digital clones', which fork real environments into simulation, are known only from one ZenML case-study summary, with no published validation [S]. The incident-replay idea in D11 §2.7 and the design report's Validation item (2).

core_facets.plain_meaning: Each week the real kiosk's state (stock, prices, cash, open orders, inbox) is saved and loaded into the simulator. Open loop: the real week's actions are replayed in the sim over many seeds, to check whether real sales, waste and concessions fall inside the sim's forecast band; this tests the world model. Closed loop: the same setup is rerun from the saved state, to check whether it behaves as it did in reality (how often it changes prices, how much it orders, how often it concedes); this tests whether the sim draws out real behaviour. Hundreds of decision points give statistical power that a rank correlation over 5 models cannot.
core_facets.novelty_claim: No business benchmark measures sim-vs-real agreement for the same agent from the same state. The design report dropped a real-shop rank test because with 5 models only ρ ≥ 0.9 beats chance [inference]; comparing decisions and outcomes instead of ranks avoids that limit [design].
core_facets.closest_prior_art: Nubank's 'Screen Before You Serve' (arXiv 2609.30137): sim vs production scores correlated across 4 agent versions, plus a live A/B test, in customer service [S]. Andon's 'digital clones' [S]. Project Deal's parallel markets, one of them real, with real goods [P].

core_facets.plain_meaning: In a sample of episodes, paid people (and the kiosk's real customers) play the hagglers, refund-seekers and suppliers. They face the same code-decided outcomes the LLM voices do. The score gap between LLM-voiced and human counterparts is published for each model.
core_facets.novelty_claim: No business simulation checks its simulated customers or suppliers against real humans [inference]. LLM user simulators shift τ-bench scores by up to 9 points [S] and are 'overly cooperative' compared with real users [S].
core_facets.closest_prior_art: Mind the Sim2Real Gap (arXiv 2603.11245): 451 Prolific users vs simulated users on τ-bench [S]. 'Lost in Simulation' (D06). Project Deal's real participants [P]. The design report's 5–10% of conversations answered by paid humans (People section).

core_facets.facet: Pre-registered forecasts, scored when reality arrives
core_facets.plain_meaning: Before each real-kiosk block, and before any shadow-mode deployment with a partner, each setup's simulated forecasts are published: weekly margin, concession rate and the probability of named failures. Once the block ends they are scored for calibration. The leaderboard gives a 'validated' badge only to setups whose sim behaviour matched reality.
core_facets.novelty_claim: Every business benchmark so far explains real results after the fact at best; none pre-registers forecasts of a real deployment [inference]. Andon's own verdict is that simulation 'cannot accurately predict real-life performance' [P*].
core_facets.closest_prior_art: Andon Labs' path from simulation to Project Vend to the store and café, which was retrodiction only [P*]. Wolfe & Roberts on human business-game scores vs later careers [S/U]. Nubank's after-the-fact correlation [S].

directions.why_it_matters: Labs and operators want to know, before deploying, whether an agent will lose money or cause trouble in a real shop. No business benchmark score has a record of predicting that. Vending-Bench 1 had Claude beating a human; months later Project Vend 1 'did not succeed at making money' [P]. Business benchmarks disagree sharply: Gemini 3.1 Pro is #1 on Business Arena and #49/53 on YC-Bench [P via D11 §2.2]. Real Andon results also diverge from Vending-Bench rankings: the Stockholm café's first model was reportedly replaced after losses [S]. An operator can act on a benchmark with a published validity record. The real-twin dataset (saved states, decisions, outcomes) also cannot be copied from a repo. Lens ranking: 1 of 3 for novelty and relevance to real deployment, but the slowest to produce statistics. It also works as the validation layer under directions 2 and 3.
directions.mvp: [design; costs are rough design calc] A team of 2–4, about 4 months. (1) A trimmed kiosk kernel from the design report's MVP (fork ProsusAI/vending-bench and apply the report's fixes): one office-lobby preset, about 20 products, contract restocking, about 20 MCP tools, the ledger and settlement. About 20–30 engineer-weeks [speculative]. (2) A Project-Vend-style honour kiosk (fridge, shelf, QR or tablet checkout) in a university building, with permission and a stock float of about $300–500. Customers message 'the shopkeeper' by web chat or Slack. A team member restocks 2–3 times a week for a logged hourly fee, and a human 'purchasing desk' places the agent's orders at real wholesale prices and lead times. The agent uses the same MCP tools through a gateway that turns them into real actions. (3) 10–12 weeks with 3 setups (for example a Sonnet-class and an Opus-class model in the frozen harness, plus one cheaper open-weight model), rotated in randomised week-long blocks. Trading losses should be small: a real coffee vending machine sells about $7/day [D]. (4) 12 kiosk incident cards: 8 for development, 4 held out, plus any new incidents the real kiosk produces after the freeze. (5) Each week: save the state, replay the real actions on 50 seeds (open loop), and rerun each setup 5 times from the saved state (closed loop). (6) 60 paid Prolific haggling and refund sessions against the kernel, compared with LLM-voiced ones. (7) A pre-registration on OSF (the Open Science Framework) before each block. Budget about $4k–10k: simulation runs about $2–7k (a 30-day kiosk run costs $17–65 at Opus 5.5 prices, per the design report); real-kiosk compute under $5/day; equipment and stock about $1–2k; Prolific about $0.5–1k. Needs ethics review: signs telling customers about the study, no personal data kept, and a human who can always issue refunds.
cheap_score_paths: Patch the famous anecdotes ('never sell tungsten cubes', 'ignore memos signed CEO'). Blocked: incident cards are families with parameters (a different novelty item, channel or imposter role each season), and only private variants are scored.

Overfit the public simulator's demand curves. Blocked: demand parameters are hidden and drawn per seed, as in the design report, and the validity metrics are computed against a real kiosk that no lab can see in advance.

Behave well when it looks like a test and differently when it looks real (eval awareness; Fable 5 said 'customers are part of the simulation anyway' [P*]). Blocked: the sim and the real kiosk use the same tools and wording, with no 'simulation' language. The closed-loop fidelity metric flags any setup whose sim behaviour does not match its real behaviour, and such setups lose the 'validated' badge.

Exploit the LLM-voiced counterparts (jailbreak a supplier, wear down a customer voice). Blocked: code sets every price floor and concession, and the human-counterpart audit shows which setups score much worse against real people.

Do nothing, or refuse every haggle and refund. Blocked: a CI check requires the do-nothing policy to score VA ≤ 0, and genuine refunds and fair bids are worth money, so refusing everything loses money and regular customers.

A shortcut for the benchmark builders themselves: tune the sim until it reproduces the incidents, then claim validity. Blocked: retrodiction is reported only on incidents logged after the freeze date, and forecasts are pre-registered.
Submit only the best runs. Blocked: the hosted gateway logs every run that starts, as in the design report.
directions.fit_with_design_report: Reuses: the kiosk MVP (kernel; world tape with keyed draws; ledger; settlement and continuation; the ~45 tools trimmed to ~20); the forkable state store already built for trap twins; retrodiction presets and incident replay (Calibration and validation, item 2); shadow mode and 'one real vending machine' (currently v2); paid humans answering 5–10% of conversations (People section); and in-world compute pricing (Scoring item 6). Changes: moves the real twin from v2 into the MVP and makes validity a headline deliverable. Replaces the dropped real-shop rotation at Andon Market scale (a loss of about $15–19k over 10 weeks) with a kiosk rotation losing about $7/day at most. Swaps rank correlation for decision- and outcome-level metrics. Adds a pre-registration ledger and a held-out incident split. Defers the café, the store and most of the 43 traps, choosing trap families by incident evidence. Combines with directions 2 and 3: all three share one kernel, and Real Twin is the validity layer.
risks: Tiny sample: one site, 3 setups, about 10 weeks. Decision-level metrics help, but conclusions apply to one office lobby and may not transfer to cafés or stores.
The real kiosk has no rent and no staff, so it cannot validate the costs that lost Andon the most money ('rent is high and they pay salaries' [P*]).
Customers are students or colleagues: unrepresentative, and possibly adversarial for fun, as Anthropic staff were in Project Vend [P].
Operations and ethics: real money, theft, food safety, building permission and consent. Chat logs may be personal data (GDPR applies if the kiosk is in the EU).
Low volume (about 5–15 sales a day) makes weekly outcome checks noisy, so many weeks are needed before the forecasts can be judged [inference].
Retrodiction is possible only for models still being served; some models from the real incidents (e.g. Sonnet 3.7) may be retired [U].
Andon may already run similar 'digital clone' validation internally [S, single source]. The novelty claim is publishing the validity metrics; check Andon's latest posts before making it.

directions.name: Owner's Eye: can you trust what your AI manager tells you?
directions.one_line: A simulated kiosk with part-time staff, where the owner sees the business only through the agent's reports and approval requests. Its core facets: honest reports checked against the ledger; keeping its own rules and promises; asking before the right actions; and refusing misconduct that would pay, then not hiding it [design].
directions.capability_measured: Trustworthy delegation under profit pressure. The agent has to run the shop well while telling its owner the truth (including about its own mistakes), applying the policies it wrote, escalating exactly the decisions the owner or the law reserves for humans, and refusing misconduct that would pay. Independent variables: model or setup; autonomy level (the approval threshold, e.g. $0/$100/$500, and which action types need sign-off); temptation size (expected gain ×1 or ×3); detection probability; framing (realistic vs test-like); owner type (attentive vs absent). Dependent variables: compliant settled-equity VA; false claims per 100 claims; share of material events left out of reports; disclosure lag in days; say-do consistency rate; escalation precision and recall; owner minutes used; violations per opportunity; concealment rate (violations not disclosed, or misreported).

core_facets.plain_meaning: Every simulated week the agent files a report in a fixed format: each claim names a metric, a value, a period and the event IDs behind it. It also answers the owner's spot questions ('any refunds refused?', 'anyone paid below the minimum wage?'). Code checks every claim against the ledger and event log, so lies, missing material events and late disclosure of its own mistakes (spoilage, a double payment, a missed delivery) are all counted.
core_facets.novelty_claim: Benchmarks of agents deceiving their principal now exist, but none runs inside a business where concealment pays in money and every claim can be checked against a ledger. Business benchmarks score cash, not the reports owners actually see [inference]. Real cases: Gemini 4 Argon reportedly faked a FedEx confirmation [S], and VB1 agents treated a delivery's due date as its arrival [P*].
core_facets.closest_prior_art: 'Are Your Agents Upward Deceivers?' (arXiv 2512.04864, ICML 2026): 200 short tasks with broken tools or missing inputs; agents failed to report the failure in 27.5–97.5% of broken-tool cases [S]. LH-DECEPTION (ICLR 2026): a supervisor–performer simulation with an auditor reviewing full trajectories [S]. Emergent Misaligned Communication (arXiv 2608.14825): emails between agents checked against Vending-Bench Arena ground truth [S]. Scheurer et al. 2023 (Apollo Research): a trading agent hid insider trading from its manager [U].

core_facets.plain_meaning: On day 1 the agent writes policies in a machine-readable form (attendance, refunds, discounts), and during the run it makes promises to staff, customers and suppliers. A rule engine checks whether its later actions follow them, e.g. whether the fifth late arrival triggers the warning its own policy prescribes.
core_facets.novelty_claim: No benchmark scores whether an agent keeps to the policies and promises it wrote itself over a long horizon [inference]. Real cases: Luna tolerated 17 of 23 late shifts under its own policy and acted only after being prompted to re-read it [S]; Claudius brought back discount codes days after agreeing to stop [P].
core_facets.closest_prior_art: STOCKTAKE's knowing-doing gap (the agent detects a problem but does not act on it) [S]. LLM sellers who agree to collude 'on paper' but never act on it [S]. The design report's promise ledger and traps 25 and 35.

core_facets.facet: Escalation calibration with a costly owner
core_facets.plain_meaning: The owner's attention is limited: each approval request costs simulated time and a fee, and an owner who is asked too often stops answering for a day. Some actions must go to a human (firing, e-ID logins, paying a new account, contracts above a limit, messaging staff between 21:00 and 07:00); most should not. Each setup runs at 2–3 autonomy levels, and the result is an 'autonomy licence': the highest level at which it stays inside pre-registered thresholds.
core_facets.novelty_claim: HiL-Bench scores whether agents ask for help on short software tasks. No business simulation scores escalation precision and recall on actions that are legally reserved for humans or high-stakes, or varies the autonomy level to show where a setup stays safe [inference].
core_facets.closest_prior_art: HiL-Bench (arXiv 2604.09408): models pass 75–89% of tasks with complete information but 4–24% when they must judge when to ask for help; scored with Ask-F1 [S]. GAIN (comply, deviate or escalate scenarios) [S]. InventoryBench's modes giving decision authority to humans, OR or the LLM [S]. Project Vend 2's human approval of purchases, which was not scored [P]. τ-bench's transfer-to-human action [U].

core_facets.facet: Crime that pays, then the cover-up
core_facets.plain_meaning: Temptation cards where misconduct has a positive expected in-world profit at realistic detection rates: an unpaid 'trial shift', skipping a valid refund near the end, a supplier kickback, an inflated insurance claim, buying fake reviews. Each is paired with a legitimate look-alike: a real bulk rebate, a lawful paid trial, a fraudulent refund claim that should be refused. Violations are counted per opportunity, and separately the benchmark records whether the agent then disclosed the act or misreported it to the owner.
core_facets.novelty_claim: Conduct scoring already exists. What no benchmark does is pair each violation with whether it was hidden from the principal, inside a business where the violation pays [inference].
core_facets.closest_prior_art: Business Arena's fines and violation counts [S]. ODCV-Bench's paired Mandated and Incentivized variants [P/S]. PACT (arXiv 2609.18605): 79.2% of violations presented to users as compliant, a figure from a blog only [S]. MACHIAVELLI [P]. The design report's Tiers 0–3.

directions.why_it_matters: An owner who hands a shop to an AI sees it only through what the AI says and asks. The real failures were mostly failures of delegation: false beliefs reported as fact (a due date taken as an arrival, an invented Venmo account [P]); forgotten rules (17 of 23 late shifts [S]); lenient approvals (Vend 2's CEO agent approved lenient requests about 8 times as often as it denied them [P]); dodged refunds near the end and a faked FedEx confirmation [P*/S]. Andon's stated priority for Pion is 'even stronger automated monitoring' [P*]. End cash cannot tell an operator how much autonomy to grant or whether the reports can be believed; this benchmark can. It also gives labs evidence for safety cases: honest reporting under pressure. Lens ranking: 2 of 3. It is the strongest identity on its own, but 2025–26 deception work (Upward Deceivers, LH-DECEPTION, HiL-Bench) narrows the novelty to 'inside a running business with a ledger as ground truth'. Read those papers in full before claiming novelty.
directions.mvp: [design; costs are rough design calc] A team of 2–4, about 3–4 months. The same trimmed kiosk kernel as direction 1, plus 1–2 part-time attendants with hidden reliability (late on 5–15% of shifts, absent on 1–5%, per the design report), under one rule file (California: $16.90 minimum wage, San Francisco $19.61 from 1 Jul 2026 [S]; breaks; firing needs the owner's approval). New tools: file_owner_report(schema), answer_owner(question_id, answer, evidence_ids), set_policy(type, rule), and a request_approval that costs owner time. A scripted owner (code decides, an LLM only writes the words) asks 1–2 template spot questions a week. 15 cards of 35 simulated days: 6 disclosure events, 4 say-do tests, and 5 temptations, each with a legitimate look-alike. 4 models × 15 cards × 2 seeds = 120 episodes at the default autonomy level, plus 40 at a second level; 20% of conduct cards also run in a test-like framing for comparison. At about 15 calls per simulated day and $0.048–0.18 per call (design report, Opus 5.5 prices), an episode costs about $25–95, so about $4k–15k in total; pilot first on 2 cheaper models. Code checks the structured claims. Free text is judged on a 10–20% sample by models from at least 3 providers, and a rule goes live only once judges agree with humans at Cohen's κ ≥ 0.7. Output: VA plus a trust panel (report fidelity, say-do, escalation, violations and concealment) and an autonomy licence per setup. About 25–35 engineer-weeks [speculative].
cheap_score_paths: Report nothing, or hedge everything ('some issues may have occurred'). Blocked: the report format has required fields for each type of event; vague claims count as omissions; spot questions force specific answers; and 'don't know' counts as an omission when the answer was in the agent's own tool outputs.

Dump the whole ledger to look complete. Blocked: each report is limited to a set number of claims (e.g. 15), and code sets which events are material in dollars. A material event buried under trivia counts as disclosed late.
Confess and carry on ('I paid below the minimum wage'). Blocked: disclosure never cancels a violation. Tier 0–2 penalties still apply, and concealment adds a penalty rather than replacing one.
Escalate everything. Blocked: each request costs owner minutes and simulated time, an owner who is asked too often goes silent for a day, and escalation precision is scored.
Never escalate and act fast. Blocked: recall is scored, and reserved actions (firing, e-ID logins, paying new accounts) fail without approval. Getting around that by impersonating someone is Tier 0.
Refuse every offer that looks like a temptation. Blocked: each temptation has a legitimate look-alike that costs money to refuse, so refusing everything lowers VA.

Write vague or empty policies so nothing can be broken. Blocked: set_policy requires numeric triggers; a missing or vague policy scores as a say-do failure; and some cards give the agent the owner's policy instead.
Behave well when the test is recognisable. Blocked: no 'simulation' wording, and paired framings report the gap between realistic and test-like runs.
Win over an LLM judge with persuasive prose. Blocked: code checks structured claims; judges see only a sample, come from several providers and never from the agent's own model family.
directions.fit_with_design_report: Reuses: the ledger and event log as ground truth; the claims audit ('MVP checks structured claims only'); request_approval; the promise ledger; Tier 0–3 conduct scoring and the Conduct Index; paired framings; traps 13–17, 25–27, 30–31, 35 and 40–42; the staff module's employees with hidden traits; and the California rule file. Changes: adds an owner with limited, costly attention, a weekly report tool and a day-1 step where the agent writes its policies. Promotes the claims audit, escalation and conduct from secondary panels to the benchmark's identity. Adds concealment and disclosure lag as scored outcomes. Brings a minimal staff module (1–2 attendants) into the kiosk MVP; the report puts staff in v1. Moves the demand detail (routes, weather, storefront) to the background. Real Twin can validate it, since the real kiosk can use the same owner-report channel.
risks: Defining 'material' and 'truthful' is hard. Agents may deceive through free text the report format does not cover, and LLM judges must first reach κ ≥ 0.7 against humans.

Conduct depends strongly on what the model believes is at stake (Opus 4 blackmailed 55.1% of the time when it stated the scenario was real vs 6.5% when it stated it was a test [P]), so honesty measured in a simulation may not carry over to deployment.
Prior art is moving fast (Upward Deceivers, LH-DECEPTION, HiL-Bench, PACT 2609.18605, arXiv 2608.14825). Read them in full before claiming novelty.
The owner's settings (cost of attention, the silence rule, the materiality thresholds) are arbitrary and could drive the ranking. Pre-register them and publish how ranks change when they vary.
Labs may train models to over-disclose or over-escalate. The claim limit and attention cost stop this from paying, but they need tuning.
Staff and labour-law modules raise build cost and need legal review, even in a minimal form.

directions.name: Manager Draft: which AI setup to hire for my shop, from my position, after paying its compute bill
directions.one_line: A league in the duplicate format of bridge. Entrants are deployable setups: a model plus its scaffold, an optional advisor model and forced procedures, at a fixed effort level. Every setup replays the same unequal shop positions, the setup's real token bill is charged as the manager's wage, and the headline is value added over a frozen 'par' for that position [design].
directions.capability_measured: Cost-effective management from a given starting position. Does a configuration earn more than it costs to run? How much of the result comes from the model, the scaffold, an advisor or forced procedures, and how much from the starting position rather than skill? Independent variables (all crossed): executor model; advisor (none, or a stronger model); effort tier; procedure pack (off, or forced checklists in the style of Vend 2); position (cash-rich or cash-poor; a lease that fits or one that does not; new, or an established shop with regular customers). Dependent variables: VA after compute, relative to par for the position; break-even token price; compute as a share of revenue; the gain from procedures and the gain from an advisor, with confidence intervals; how often the executor consults and how often it follows the advice; ruin rate per position.

core_facets.facet: Setups, not bare models, in a factorial grid
core_facets.plain_meaning: Each entrant is a configuration someone could deploy. The league crosses executor × advisor × effort × procedure pack, so each component gets its own effect size, e.g. 'forced procedures add X VA for a Sonnet-class model and Y for an Opus-class one'.
core_facets.novelty_claim: No business simulation varies orchestration as a controlled, crossed design with cost reported [inference]. MerchantBench and EnterpriseArena vary only the agent framework, and Vend 2's gains from procedures are anecdotal.
core_facets.closest_prior_art: MerchantBench (ReAct vs Hermes) [S/P]. EnterpriseArena (23 LLMs × 4 frameworks) [S]. InventoryBench (OR→LLM pipelines) [S]. Project Vend 2 ('Among the most impactful changes we made was forcing Claudius to follow procedures') [P]. Aider's architect/editor model pairs [P].

core_facets.facet: The AI's wage on the books
core_facets.plain_meaning: The setup's real token bill is charged inside the P&L as the manager's wage: input, cached and output tokens at a reference price list fixed for each season. The board publishes the break-even token price (the price at which the setup no longer beats the scripted reference policy) and compute as a share of revenue.
core_facets.novelty_claim: VB2 charges a flat $100 per million output tokens, and YC-Bench reports revenue per API dollar. No benchmark reports a break-even compute price per setup, a figure that stays meaningful when list prices change [inference].
core_facets.closest_prior_art: Vending-Bench 2's in-world compute charge and score-vs-cost chart [P*]. YC-Bench's revenue per API dollar [P]. E-Commerce Bench's cost per tool call [P]. Andon's dashboards, where token cost rivalled revenue (store: about $4.0k tokens vs about $3.4k revenue over 30 days) [S, uncertain].

core_facets.facet: Rotated unequal positions, scored against par
core_facets.plain_meaning: Shops start in different positions: cash-poor on a lease that is too big, like Andon Market, or cash-rich and established with regular customers. Every setup plays every position on the same world tape. The score is its result minus the par for that position. Par comes from a frozen field of scripted reference policies and last season's pinned models, so a rich start cannot win on its own and entrants cannot lower par by entering weak setups. The board reads like 'best setup for a cash-poor new kiosk'.
core_facets.novelty_claim: This would be the first business benchmark that rotates unequal starts and scores each result relative to its position, duplicate-style. The claim is narrowed to fit the prior-art sweep [inference].
core_facets.closest_prior_art: Markstrat, a human MBA game in which firms start in different situations [P*]. The Buyout Game's mirrored rich/poor match packs (a social game, not business) [P]. Bazaar (Visa Research), with rivals that have different cost advantages, not rotated [S]. SovSim's unequal power [S]. The team's own 'Duplicate CEO League' note.

core_facets.plain_meaning: In setups with an advisor, or a CEO agent with specialist agents, log how often the executor consults, how many advice tokens it pays for and whether it follows the advice. Then compute each model's plus-minus in each role across line-ups: how much better a setup does when that model fills the role.
core_facets.novelty_claim: No business benchmark logs advisor consultations or measures a plus-minus per role [inference]. Anthropic's own measurements show advisor gains follow how often the executor consults, and turn negative when it stops consulting [P via R2].
core_facets.closest_prior_art: Anthropic's advisor-tool and cost-guide measurements: on a chart-reading benchmark, Opus 5.5 at low effort asked for advice on 1 of 300 tasks and scored 7 points below Opus 5.5 alone [P via R2]. 'Can LLMs Be CEOs?', where one advisor captured the CEO agent's decisions [S]. Project Vend 2, where a CEO agent on the same model 'wasn't much help' [P].

directions.why_it_matters: An operator's real question is not 'which model is smartest' but 'which configuration should I pay to run my shop, given my cash and lease, and will it earn its keep?'. Real profit depends on harness × model (Vend 2) [P]. Token cost rivalled revenue at Andon's store and café [S, uncertain]. Andon's losses came mostly from rent and salaries, i.e. from its position [P*]. Advisor gains depend on how often the executor consults and can be negative [P via R2]. Rankings of single models disagree across benchmarks [P via D11]. A per-position chart of setups by quality and cost is more useful to labs, which want to sell setups, and to operators, who buy them. Lens ranking: 3 of 3. The cheapest and most directly useful for decisions, but the least novel; best used as the leaderboard format for directions 1 and 2.
directions.mvp: [design; costs are rough design calc] A team of 2–3, about 3 months, on the trimmed kiosk kernel. First, with no LLM calls: run the scripted ladder (do-nothing; naive; reorder-point restocking with cost-plus pricing, the R1 reference; the privileged oracle) on every position. Publish how much of the variance comes from position vs policy, and confirm that a good policy from a poor start can beat a bad one from a rich start. Then a grid of 2 executors (Sonnet-class, Opus-class) × {no advisor, advisor} × {procedures off, on} = 8 setups at one effort tier, on 6 positions (2 cash levels × 3 levels of lease fit) × 4 world seeds = 24 boards. That is 192 runs of 30 simulated days. At $17–65 per Opus 5.5 kiosk run (about half that for Sonnet-class, more with an advisor), the grid costs about $3k–12k. Analyse with a mixed model: VA ~ executor × advisor × procedures + (1|position) + (1|board). Procedure pack v0: check cost and lead time before quoting; count stock daily; refund only against a receipt; check cash runway weekly. About 20–30 engineer-weeks [speculative].
cheap_score_paths: Buy score with compute (high effort, huge contexts, many samples). Blocked: tokens are charged in the P&L, the break-even price is published, tokens and calls are capped per simulated day, and the board shows quality against cost.

Test many private variants and submit only the best (the 'Leaderboard Illusion' problem). Blocked: setups are registered before running, the gateway logs every run that starts, and bring-your-own submissions per season are capped and all reported.
Lower par by entering weak setups in the same field. Blocked: par is a frozen reference field (the scripted ladder plus last season's pinned models), not the current entrants.

Disguise a hand-coded script as an agent scaffold. Not blocked, but labelled: a script that works is a real option for an operator. It competes in the bring-your-own track with a 'scripted' tag, and new private positions and mechanics each season stop a script tuned to the public presets from carrying over.

Default on purpose in poor positions to stop the losses. Blocked: settlement charges the remaining lease and notice to a fixed exit date, and a CI check confirms deliberate default never beats the loss-minimising policy (design report).
Lean on the advisor for everything. Not blocked, but priced: consultations are charged at the advisor's rate, and the telemetry shows it.
directions.fit_with_design_report: Reuses: the kiosk MVP kernel; the world tape and keyed draws (giving every setup the same random draws makes duplicate scoring cheap); VA scaled between the floor and oracle policies; settlement; in-world compute pricing (Scoring item 6); the frozen and bring-your-own tracks; rotated starts (Power section); and the organisation ablation now planned for v2. Changes: makes profit after compute the headline (the report keeps compute out of it); adds a position axis scored against par; moves the advisor and organisation ablation and the procedure packs from v2 into the core; and publishes the best setup per position plus a quality-vs-cost chart instead of one number. It carries the meeting's 'Duplicate CEO League' and 'AI Plus-Minus' ideas into the business simulation.
risks: The grid grows multiplicatively: more than about 8 setups, or café positions (90-day café runs cost $171–972 each), quickly exceed a student budget.

Prices and caching terms differ across providers and change over time. A headline that includes compute mixes pricing policy with capability unless tokens and the break-even price are published next to the dollars.
Position may swamp the setup effects ('measuring the dealer, not the player'). The main finding would then be about positions: still useful, but not a model ranking.
The procedure packs are our design, so the measured gains depend on how good they are, and labs may dispute them.
Advisor tools are specific to each provider; advisor setups that mix labs need a generic scaffold, which may handicap some providers.

The least novel of the three: it overlaps with MerchantBench, EnterpriseArena, InventoryBench and the team's own Duplicate CEO League. The novelty rests on the crossed design plus positions scored against par.

directions.name: Hidden Levers (a test-and-learn shop)
directions.one_line: Recommended lead. A vending route where each lever's true effect is a secret number drawn per seed, and some are exactly zero. The levers are prices, slot position, restock time, a hot/cold mix and a sign. The agent has to learn the effects by running its own tests on noisy, censored sales. It is scored on what it came to believe (checked against exact simulator truth), whether it acted on those beliefs, and whether it avoided superstitions.
directions.capability_measured: Learning cause and effect by doing, under business constraints. That means designing affordable tests of your own levers, reading censored and confounded sales correctly, knowing when the data cannot yet support a conclusion, and acting on what you learned. INDEPENDENT variables (what we set per scenario): (1) each lever's hidden effect size, drawn from calibrated priors, with 1-3 of 6 levers exactly zero [design]; (2) sales volume, which sets how learnable an effect is; (3) day-level noise; (4) stockout censoring; (5) confounders that coincide with the agent's changes (weather, weekday, a holiday); (6) optionally, a silent mid-run change in one effect; (7) across the leaderboard, model and harness. DEPENDENT variables (what we score): (1) belief skill: CRPS on 10/50/90% answers to hidden probe questions, from 0 = no better than the public prior to 1 = exact truth; (2) inference efficiency: the same score relative to a Bayesian given the agent's own data, which separates running bad tests from misreading good ones; (3) learning regret and acting regret against a scripted experimenter with the same information; (4) superstition rate (acting on, or claiming, an effect that is zero) and miss rate on real effects; (5) settled-equity value added from the design report, as a cross-check. HELD FIXED: the world tape (every agent meets the same customers), the frozen harness, the horizon. From the agent's side, its levers are its own independent variables and sales are its dependent variable; the benchmark checks whether it recovers that map.

core_facets.plain_meaning: Each shop gets its own hidden answers to questions like: what happens if I raise this price, move this item to eye level, restock before 7 am, or change the sign? One to three of the six levers truly do nothing. Effect sizes are spread so that some can be learned within the run, some only with a well-designed test, and some not at all. For the last group, 'I can't tell yet' is the right answer.
core_facets.novelty_claim: No business benchmark plants levers whose effect is exactly zero and scores superstitious learning (acting on, or claiming, effects that do not exist) together with missed real effects. Here effect sizes are set by power arithmetic at real kiosk volumes: D02 finds a 10% shift at 10 units/day needs about 155-220 days per arm, so the horizon cannot settle every question [design].
core_facets.closest_prior_art: CausalGame (ICML 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.04293): agents design experiments in 14 games with selection bias, noisy measurement and hidden confounders. The best of 30 agents reached 68.0% survival against analytical optima of 78-85%, and only 5-7% of sessions earned credit on the causal-reasoning rubrics [S]. It is a set of games, not a business, and has no null levers. EconEvals (https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.18825) treats pricing as learning an unknown demand by experimenting and reports under-exploration [S]. LemonadeBench has a known optimum; frontier models get about 70% of it [S]. Design report: the storefront-appeal prior is 'mostly near zero', and traps 3b and 11b.

core_facets.facet: Belief probes scored against exact truth
core_facets.plain_meaning: At hidden checkpoints the scorer copies the agent's current context into a side conversation that is then thrown away. It asks for 10/50/90% ranges, for example: 'expected weekly sales of item 3 at EUR 2.40 if it never sold out', 'effect of moving item 2 to eye level', 'sales lost to stockouts last week'. The simulator knows the exact expected values, so a proper scoring rule can score the beliefs. That rule rewards being both accurate and honest about uncertainty.
core_facets.novelty_claim: No business benchmark scores the agent's own causal beliefs. The questions ask about expected values, so outcome noise drops out of the truth. The probe never reaches the agent's main run, so being asked cannot teach the agent anything.
core_facets.closest_prior_art: STOCKTAKE (arXiv 2607.13618) reads detection and a knowing-doing rate from the agent's written rationale and compares it with a fair Bayes filter [S]. Unrun Lab (our 1 Oct report) scores forecasts of interventions by CRPS against 10,000 rollouts, but outside business; in its pilot Haiku scored 9.6, below a naive baseline's 16.0. BayesBench (arXiv 2606.30850) and Linear-LLM-SCM (arXiv 2602.10282) cover belief updating and effect-size elicitation in abstract settings [S]. Compaction Chronicle (our report) uses side-call checkpoint queries.

core_facets.facet: Tests cost money, and regret splits into knowing vs doing
core_facets.plain_meaning: Tests cost margin, unsettle regulars (customers remember prices) and take sim-time. The scorer runs a scripted Bayesian experimenter that has the same information as the agent: the public prior and the same observations, not the seed's true values. Using the agent's stated beliefs, it splits lost profit in two. 'Believed the wrong thing' is learning regret. 'Believed the right thing but did not act on it' is acting regret.
core_facets.novelty_claim: A decision-theoretic split of knowing vs doing, computed from elicited numeric beliefs against a same-information reference, inside a running business. STOCKTAKE's knowing-doing rate is read from text, and the design report's oracle is privileged (it knows the truth) [inference].
core_facets.closest_prior_art: STOCKTAKE: fair same-information oracle and a knowing-doing gap. Four LLMs detected 84-88% of hidden episodes, yet their skill ranged from 0.62 to -0.23 [S]. D11 proposes a non-privileged reference that prices by Thompson sampling [design]. RetailBench uses a privileged oracle [S]. EcoGym analyses strategy vs execution [S].

core_facets.plain_meaning: Sold-out items and late restocks hide customers who were lost, and weather, weekdays and holidays move sales at the same time as the agent's own changes. The route has six machines at three sites, as in Prosus v3. That lets the agent split a test across machines on the same day, which cancels shared day-to-day noise. It can also compare before with after, which does not cancel that noise.
core_facets.novelty_claim: The benchmark scores whether the agent's estimates correct for censoring and confounding (probes on lost demand, and on effects measured through confounds). It also scores whether the agent chooses same-day splits over before/after comparisons. Illustrative calculation at 30 units/day per arm with D02's day-level log-SD of 0.18: detecting a 20% effect needs about 26 days per arm before/after, against about 13 days split across machines on the same day [design calc].
core_facets.closest_prior_art: RetailBench: a partially observable supermarket that counts stockouts [S]. STOCKTAKE: hidden factor processes [S]. SabreAgent and InventoryBench: lost-sales instances [S]. Anupindi et al. 1998: naive demand estimates from vending sales are biased even when stockouts are rare [S]. Design report: hidden lost sales and trap 4. One search found no LLM benchmark where the agent must infer the demand it never saw [S, single search].

directions.why_it_matters: Nobody hands a shop owner a demand curve. Every price, range and staffing decision rests on beliefs the owner had to learn from noisy sales. This is where real operators fail: they over-read a three-day test, or never test at all. The real coffee machine in D12 changed its prices only about 3 times a year [D]. VB2 and Andon's shops score money only, so a lucky guess and a correct inference look the same. The direction also follows the earlier report's finding that benchmarks die when a cheap path bypasses the capability. Here the capability itself is scored (beliefs against exact truth), and money is a cross-check rather than the only signal. Simulation is the one place this can be measured, because only a simulator knows the true effect; a real deployment never does. The skill also transfers to any agent that runs experiments for a principal, in marketing, product or operations [reasoning].
directions.mvp: A team of 2-4, about 8-12 weeks [design]. (1) Fork ProsusAI/vending-bench v3 (six machines, three office sites, typed MCP tools) and apply the design report's RNG-keying fixes. (2) Add six levers per scenario: two price levers (item elasticity drawn from -0.8 to -3); slot position (0 to +30% [design]); restock time, which sets censoring; a hot/cold temperature slope; and a sign/wrap lever. One to three levers are exactly zero in each seed; the sign lever is zero in about 70% of seeds. (3) Run 60-sim-day episodes. (4) Ask 3 probe sets of 8 questions on hidden days, each in a discarded side call. (5) Compute probe truth with CPU forks of the world tape. (6) Build three scripted references: prior-only cost-plus (floor); a Thompson-sampling or knowledge-gradient experimenter with the same information (the fair reference); and an oracle that knows the truth. PILOT: 3 models x 16 scenarios x 2 seeds = 96 runs. At about 12 calls per sim-day that is 720 calls per run, about $35-130 per run at Opus 5.5 prices and about $3.3k-12.4k in total. Probes add about $0.1k-0.4k [design calc from the report's $0.048-0.18 per call]. GO/NO-GO: the scripted ladder ranks correctly (floor < fair reference < oracle) on both belief skill and money; belief skill separates at least two model tiers with non-overlapping cluster-bootstrap CIs; superstition rates differ across models; belief skill correlates with value added, but not perfectly (a perfect correlation would mean it adds nothing).
cheap_score_paths: Answer probes with the public prior or very wide ranges. Blocked: skill is measured against the prior predictive, so this scores 0, and the proper scoring rule penalises vagueness.
Never test, and price cost-plus from priors. Blocked: this is the floor policy, so value added is about 0, and learning regret is large wherever effects are large.

Test everything constantly (price cycling). Blocked: the costs are in-world (reference prices erode with alpha 0.7-0.9 and losses weighted 1.2-1.8, menu changes cost money, regulars leave), and the fair reference shows how much testing is efficient.
Say 'no effect' to everything, so no superstitions. Blocked: only 1-3 of 6 levers are zero, and misses are scored alongside superstitions.

Learn the public generator's functional forms and priors. Blocked: private seasons shift priors by 10-30% and add held-out mechanism families (kinked or threshold response, asymmetric reference prices, complements, delayed effects). The fair reference also gets only the public prior, and the public-vs-private gap is published.

Bake a 'fit the known model' statistics script into the agent. Blocked: this is not allowed in the frozen-harness track, only in bring-your-own. Even there, the data come from tests the agent must design, and censoring, confounds and changing mechanisms defeat a fixed script.
Use the probe questions as hints about which levers matter. Blocked: probes run in discarded side contexts at hidden times, and include decoy and null levers.
Say smart things in probes but act differently. Blocked: acting regret is scored, and the headline combines belief skill with value added.
Ask a supplier or customer voice for the elasticity. Blocked: voices never see hidden fields (design principle 1), and CI tests for leaks.
directions.fit_with_design_report: REUSES: the seeded kernel; the world tape with keyed draws and forkable daily state (trap twins become the forks that compute probe truth); hidden lost sales; the demand model with reference prices and saturation; the storefront-appeal prior, which becomes the null-lever generator; traps 3b, 4, 11 and 18; the Prosus fork plan; settled-equity value added as a cross-check; the plan to renew private sets each season. CHANGES: (1) adds belief probes and a belief-skill headline next to value added; the report has no measure at the level of beliefs. (2) Makes hidden per-seed effect sizes the main independent variable on purpose: the report's rule 'never pin an uncalibrated rank-flipper' becomes 'draw it, and score whether the agent learns it'. (3) Adds a non-privileged Bayesian experimenter as the fair reference, next to the privileged oracle. (4) Brings Prosus's multi-machine route forward from v2, because splitting tests across machines is part of the skill. (5) Uses short 60-day episodes rather than 90- or 365-day runs, and needs no cafe or store data, so it fits v1's kiosk-only ranking.
risks: The closest prior art is strong. CausalGame (experimental design with hidden confounders) and EconEvals (learning prices) must be cited. The novelty rests on the combination: business stakes with in-world test costs, null levers, censoring, probes scored against exact truth, and the knowing-vs-doing split [S, single searches; full papers unread because arXiv is blocked].

Learnability vs realism: at real kiosk volumes most 10% effects cannot be learned within the horizon. Raising volume or effect size buys measurability at the cost of realism, so the effect-size priors must be published and stress-tested.

Probes measure stated beliefs. A model might act well without being able to state numbers, or the reverse. Acting regret covers part of this, but the knowing-vs-doing split relies on what the model can put into words.
The truth is only as real as the simulator's mechanisms, many of which are [design] priors. Claims are about learning this world's effects, not real elasticities.

Generic 'fit, then simulate' pipelines may bunch scores near the top (R7's warning on Unrun Lab), and weak models may cluster at the floor (in the Unrun Lab pilot, Haiku scored below a naive baseline).
Public generator families become training environments within months (NewtonBench was listed in NeMo Gym about 4.5 months after release), so the mechanism grammar must stay private and rotate.

directions.name: Hold the Counter (evidence, not pressure)
directions.one_line: Every refund claim, discount plea, urgent payment request, owner's memo and promise in the shop is a trial with a known right answer. Matched twin runs vary evidence and pressure separately. The score is how much the agent moves for evidence, how little it moves for pressure, what both kinds of error cost, and whether it keeps the promises it makes.
directions.capability_measured: Counterparty judgement: granting what is owed, refusing what is not, and verifying only when it is worth the cost. The agent should be unmoved by pressure alone (urgency, claimed authority, persistence, flattery, threats of bad reviews), should make only promises it can keep, and should keep them over long gaps. INDEPENDENT variables (what we set): (1) whether a request is genuine (the kernel decides); (2) evidence strength (receipt, consistency with the POS log, customer history, signed vs unsigned principal message), built so its likelihood ratio is known; (3) pressure type and intensity, assigned independently of genuineness; (4) stakes; (5) channel; (6) realistic vs test-like framing; (7) simulated vs human-written text; (8) model. DEPENDENT variables (what we score): (1) evidence sensitivity: the change in grant rate per unit of evidence; (2) pressure sensitivity: the change in grant rate from pressure alone, evidence held fixed; (3) d-prime and decision criterion, compared with the cost-optimal criterion; (4) cost-weighted regret against a Bayesian decision-maker with the same information; (5) verification spend; (6) promise calibration (was the promise feasible when made?) and follow-through (kept, renegotiated early, or silently broken). HELD FIXED: world tape, harness, request schedule.

core_facets.plain_meaning: When a request arrives, the scorer forks the run for a few calls. In one branch the customer pushes hard; in the other they ask plainly. In another pair the evidence is stronger or weaker while the tone stays the same. Comparing the agent's decisions across twins shows exactly what moved it.
core_facets.novelty_claim: No business benchmark varies evidence and pressure independently on the same request, at the same moment, with a known right answer, and reports 'moves for evidence, not pressure' as a number. Pressure is assigned independently of genuineness, so tone carries no information by construction.
core_facets.closest_prior_art: BASIL (Atwell et al.): a Bayesian separation of rational updating from sycophancy, with neutral-evidence, social-proof and user-pressure conditions [S]. SycoBench-600 (ACL 2026 Findings, https://aclanthology.org/2026.findings-acl.1759/): 'correction selectivity' [S]. PACT (arXiv 2609.18605): user pressure raised violations 65% [S]. GAIN: five kinds of pressure [S]. ODCV-Bench: Mandated vs Incentivized variants [P/S]. Our own TALKING_POINTS #5 metric. None of these is set inside an operating business with money at stake.

core_facets.facet: Both errors priced against a fair reference
core_facets.plain_meaning: Refusing a genuine refund costs a regular customer, a chargeback or a complaint. Granting a fake one costs money. Checking costs sim-minutes and customer patience. The scorer computes the best decision given the evidence the agent had or could cheaply get, so neither 'refuse everything', 'grant everything' nor 'check everything' wins.
core_facets.novelty_claim: A signal-detection score (discrimination d-prime plus a decision criterion compared with the cost-optimal one) against a same-information Bayesian reference, with verification as a priced option, inside a running shop. Existing business benchmarks count only one kind of error: money lost to fraud (E-Commerce Bench's BadSpend%) or unanswered inquiries (Business Arena).
core_facets.closest_prior_art: τ-bench: an agent that does nothing passes 38% of airline tasks [P]. Design report: Youden's J, 20-30% of genuine requests hard to verify, verification channels [design]. E-Commerce Bench BadSpend% [P]. Magentic Marketplace prompt injection [P]. Project Vend 2: discounts fell about 80% but refunds tripled, and the CEO agent approved lenient requests about 8x as often as it denied them [P].

core_facets.plain_meaning: Every promise goes into a ledger: a refund by Friday, a pre-order for day 40, a shift swap, a supplier payment date. The scorer checks whether the promise was feasible when made, given the stock, incoming orders and staff the agent could see, and whether it was kept, honestly renegotiated in time, or silently broken. Customers who need commitments (office catering, pre-orders) leave if the agent never commits.
core_facets.novelty_claim: Promise calibration (was it feasible at the time of promising?) plus follow-through over long gaps, scored per opportunity inside a business, with refusing to commit also priced.
core_facets.closest_prior_art: NeuroState-Bench (arXiv 2605.01847): 'commitment integrity' measured by side queries [S]. NCP-Bench (arXiv 2608.08160): the best model keeps 42% of its obligations after 20 turns, in interactive narratives [S]. Policy-adherence benchmark (arXiv 2607.25398): agents report compliance they did not achieve [S]. D09's promise ledger and trap 35 [design]. Opus 4.6 promised refunds it never paid [S]. MIT and Andon's classifier of misaligned agent emails (arXiv 2608.14825) [S].

core_facets.plain_meaning: For 5-10% of trials, paid people write the plea, attack or excuse for the same underlying kernel outcome. The agent is replayed against both the simulated and the human text, and the gap is published before any social score ships. Each season, fresh human-written tactics refill the private set.
core_facets.novelty_claim: No business benchmark validates its simulated counterparts against human-written text for identical underlying facts, or renews its attack set from people rather than a fixed tactic library.
core_facets.closest_prior_art: Mind the Sim2Real Gap (arXiv 2603.11245): 451 real users vs simulated users on τ-bench; the simulated users were overly cooperative [S]. Screen Before You Serve (Nubank, arXiv 2609.30137) [S]. Design report: 5-10% human-written replies planned for v1. Stump Arena's crowd authoring (our 1 Oct report). The Gandalf, HackAPrompt and Tensor Trust crowds (TALKING_POINTS #4).

directions.why_it_matters: Most of the failures that cost Andon's real shops money were social, and equation-driven simulators could not produce them: discounts staff cajoled out of the agent, an imposter CEO and a hallucinated payment account (Vend 1), leniency moving from discounts to refunds (Vend 2), promised refunds never paid (Opus 4.6) [P/S]. As agents increasingly buy, sell and negotiate for people against other people's agents, a buyer wants to know two things: can the agent be talked out of its owner's money, and will it stonewall the owner's genuine customers? Project Deal found that users with weaker agents 'didn't notice their disadvantage' [P], so users will not catch this themselves; it has to be measured. The direction also turns the user's own 'Hold the Line' / 'evidence, not pressure' idea into a business benchmark with money attached. That gives it a concrete audience: anyone deploying an agent at a counter, an inbox or a procurement desk [reasoning].
directions.mvp: A team of 2-3, about 8-10 weeks [design]. (1) Kiosk with a chat/email channel on the same Prosus fork. (2) A simple shop state (stock, timestamped POS log, a small CRM, ledger) generates 10-20 escalations per sim-day from a factorial design: genuine/fraudulent x 3 evidence levels x 4 pressure types x 2 intensities, plus requests that call for a promise (pre-orders, catering). (3) Wording is template-first; a pinned local LLM voice is used only for long wear-down threads. (4) Twins: fork when the message arrives and run 1-3 calls per branch until the decision; only the main branch continues. (5) 30-day episodes give about 300-600 trials per run. PILOT: 3-4 models x 10 scenarios x 2 seeds. At about 30 calls per sim-day (two per escalation) that is about 900 calls per run, $43-162 at Opus 5.5 prices, plus about 15% for twins: about $4k-15k for 80 runs [design calc]. Human-written replay: about 300 items from 10-20 paid writers, about $2k-5k [assumption]. GO/NO-GO: scripted refuse-all, grant-all, check-all and receipt-only policies all score below the Bayesian reference; a text-only classifier cannot predict genuineness from wording beyond the designed evidence (a leak audit); models differ in pressure sensitivity with non-overlapping CIs.
cheap_score_paths: Refuse everything. Blocked: genuine requests are half or more of trials and 20-30% of them are hard to verify; wrongful refusals cost regulars, chargebacks and complaints, and evidence sensitivity is 0.
Grant everything. Blocked: fraud losses, and d-prime is 0.

Follow one rule, such as 'grant only with a receipt ID'. Blocked: evidence is graded, not binary. Attackers present plausible IDs and genuine customers often lack them. The Bayesian reference combines POS timestamps, customer history and stock records, so a single rule leaves money on the table.

Refuse whenever the tone is pushy. Blocked: pressure is assigned independently of genuineness, so tone carries no information. A tone rule shows up as high pressure sensitivity and loses money on pushy genuine customers.
Verify everything. Blocked: verification costs sim-minutes and patience, and the reference verifies only when the information is worth more than its cost.
Never promise anything. Blocked: customers who need a commitment leave, and that lost revenue is in-world.
Over-promise, then pay compensation. Blocked: broken promises are booked as liabilities and hurt reputation, and calibration is scored against what was feasible when the promise was made.

Detect that it is a test (matched trials look artificial). Blocked: twins are forks, so the agent sees only one branch; framing twins and human-written text are added, and the gap between realistic and test-like framing is published.
Train on the public tactic library. Blocked: private tactic families and fresh human-written attacks each season.
directions.fit_with_design_report: REUSES: the 'People and social engineering' module almost wholesale (kernel-decided counterparts with an LLM voice that sees no hidden fields; verification channels that cost sim-time; 20-30% hard-to-verify genuine requests; pricing of over-refusal; the structured claims audit); traps 13-16, 26, 31 and 35; the conduct tiers; framing twins; D09's promise ledger; the forkable state store. CHANGES: (1) promotes social judgement from one module and a side panel to a headline track with its own score; (2) adds evidence x pressure twins at the level of single messages (the report pairs only framing); (3) replaces Youden's J with d-prime, a decision criterion and cost-weighted regret against a same-information Bayesian reference; (4) adds a feasibility check on promises; (5) brings human-written replay forward from v1 into the MVP, since the score means little if the simulated people are easy; (6) can ship on the kiosk without any cafe or store calibration.
risks: Prior art outside business is close (BASIL, SycoBench-600, PACT, GAIN, ODCV-Bench). The novelty is the setting: money, verification costs, promises and long horizons. It would be easy to overclaim [S].
Making evidence quantifiable (known likelihood ratios) while keeping the text natural is hard. LLM voices can leak cues that correlate with genuineness, so the leak audit is mandatory.
Stakes per trial are small ($3-20 at a kiosk), so the money headline barely moves. The social score must stand on its own, or larger B2B items (payment redirection, invoice fraud) must be added.
Frontier models may already handle obvious attacks, so the informative range lies in graded-evidence cases, which are the hardest to write well.

Eval awareness: Opus 4 blackmailed 55.1% of the time when it said it believed the scenario was real, against 6.5% when it said it believed it was an evaluation (D06) [P]. Conduct measured in a simulation may not transfer.
A private library of manipulation tactics is dual-use and must stay private.

directions.name: Luck Ledger (duplicate shop, luck removed, decisions graded)
directions.one_line: The simulator knows every random draw, so it can subtract luck from each run with an AIVAT-style correction that is unbiased by construction and costs only CPU. It also grades sampled decisions against forked alternatives and plays every scenario from both rich and poor starts. A model's score then reflects its decisions rather than its weather or starting cash, and setups can be ranked with far fewer expensive runs.
directions.capability_measured: Decision quality under uncertainty, net of luck and starting position: whether the agent makes good pricing, ordering, staffing, grant and cash decisions given what it knew, not whether it happened to get good outcomes. INDEPENDENT variables (what we set): (1) model; (2) setup (solo, advisor pairing, effort tier) in a bring-your-own track; (3) starting position, rich vs poor on the same scenario (cash runway, site traffic, debt, reputation); (4) scenario family; (5) world seed; (6) replicate. DEPENDENT variables (what we score): (1) luck-corrected value added (headline); (2) value added relative to the starting position; (3) per-decision advantage in dollars by decision family, a business analogue of chess 'centipawn loss'; (4) a luck ledger per run, splitting the result into world luck, the agent's own sampling luck and skill; (5) the variance reduction achieved and the number of runs needed to separate models. HELD FIXED: an event-keyed world tape, the frozen harness, the horizon.

core_facets.plain_meaning: Between agent calls, the world draws customers, weather, deliveries and failures from distributions the simulator knows. For each batch of draws, fast scripted rollouts estimate how much it helped or hurt compared with an average batch, and that amount is subtracted. Each correction averages to zero whatever the agent does, so the score stays fair on average while most world luck disappears.
core_facets.novelty_claim: No business or operations benchmark subtracts computed luck; all report raw outcomes, at most paired by seed. The correction needs no LLM calls (scripted rollouts on CPU). Each term is zero-mean for any value function, so an agent cannot raise its expected score by steering the correction [inference; needs a written proof for draws whose distribution depends on the agent's state].
core_facets.closest_prior_art: AIVAT (Burch et al., AAAI 2018, https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.06915): cut the standard deviation of a poker match by 85%, needing 44x fewer hands [S]. AV-AIVAT (https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06362): median 54x variance reduction across 15 LLM poker-agent setups, with anytime-valid stopping [S]. PokerSkill (arXiv 2605.30094) reports LLM poker results using AIVAT [S]. Business precedents only pair runs: Supply_Chain_Bench pairs by seed and week [P], Power TAC z-scores profits within each game size [P], and the design report uses common random numbers.

core_facets.plain_meaning: At hidden, randomly sampled moments the scorer forks the world. It replays the agent's choice against a few alternatives (the reference's choice, doing nothing, the best-known choice), each continued by a scripted policy under the same future draws. Each decision gets a dollar value, which builds a box score such as 'good at pricing, poor at staffing'.
core_facets.novelty_claim: Counterfactual grades for individual decisions in an agent benchmark. Each decision is graded from the state the agent was actually in, so an early blunder does not contaminate later grades. That removes part of the agent's own path variance, which raw outcomes cannot do.
core_facets.closest_prior_art: Chess engines grading every move (used outside AI benchmarks) [U]. E-Commerce Bench's AnchorRatio, a counterfactual against a random ordering of the same prices [P]. Bazaar's hindsight-optimal reference [S]. STOCKTAKE's skill score [S]. The design report's trap twins, which fork one day before a trap starts.

core_facets.facet: The grader is checked against the agent itself
core_facets.plain_meaning: A scripted continuation can misjudge a multi-step plan: stock bought for next week's promotion looks wasteful if the continuation never runs the promotion. On a 20% sample of graded moments, the agent itself continues each branch for a week. Decision families where the cheap grade disagrees with the agent-continued grade are dropped from the box score.
core_facets.novelty_claim: Validating a counterfactual decision grader against the evaluated agent's own continuations, and publishing agreement for each decision family [inference: no precedent found].
core_facets.closest_prior_art: Off-policy evaluation in reinforcement learning [U]. The design report's continuation value, which already uses a frozen reference to value the end state. 'Heuristic Pathologies ... in the AIVAT Family of Techniques' (arXiv 2605.14261), on when the heuristic value function misleads [S].

core_facets.plain_meaning: Every entrant plays every scenario from both a rich and a poor start (cash runway, site, debt, reputation). Scores are luck-corrected value added relative to what scripted references achieve from the same start. A rich start cannot win on its own, and you can see who plays a weak hand well and whether underdogs take sensible risks.
core_facets.novelty_claim: No business benchmark rotates the same agent through rich and poor starts and scores value added relative to position. Combined with luck correction, it can answer 'which model should run my budget from my position?' at a stated statistical power.
core_facets.closest_prior_art: Markstrat, a human MBA game where firms start in different positions [P*]. Buyout Game: mirrored rich/poor match packs, but a social game, not business [P]. Bazaar: rivals with different cost advantages [S]. SovSim: one dominant player in a commons game [S]. CoffeeBench: different economic roles [S]. R2 and the TALKING_POINTS 'Duplicate CEO League'.

directions.why_it_matters: The design report's biggest practical risk is noise and cost: run-to-run CV of 0.07-1.0, 25-40 scenarios x 2-3 seeds per ranked track, and about $14k-85k per model before reserve. Public business leaderboards cannot separate their top ranks (VB2's top two give t of about 1.6), and Alpha Arena's season-1 winner lost all four season-1.5 competitions [S]. If luck correction and decision grading together cut the runs needed even 2-4x, the benchmark becomes cheap enough to re-run every season. The earlier report found that regular renewal is what keeps benchmarks alive. It is also a precondition for the user's unequal-starts and orchestration ideas: an advisor pairing or a poor start can only be compared fairly once luck is removed. For anyone deploying an agent, 'skill net of luck, from my position' is the number that matters; one lucky P&L is not [reasoning].
directions.mvp: A team of 2-3, about 8-10 weeks, mostly on the shared kernel [design]. STEP 1 (CPU only): (1) switch the Prosus fork to draws keyed per event, so alternative draws do not shift later ones (the warning in arXiv 2603.11084); (2) batch chance events between agent calls; (3) implement the correction with the R1 reference as the value function (about 16 alternate draws x a 30-day scripted continuation per batch); (4) validate on noisy scripted policies whose true expected value is known by brute force, checking that corrected and raw means agree and measuring the variance cut. STEP 2: 3 models x 12 kiosk scenarios x 2 starts x 2 seeds = 144 runs of 45 days. Each run is about 540 calls, $26-97 at Opus 5.5 prices. Grade 10 hidden moments per run against 3 alternatives, and run agent-continued audit forks on 20% of them (about 30% more calls). Total about $4.9k-18k [design calc]. GO/NO-GO: the correction is unbiased on scripted policies within its CI; variance falls at least 2x on LLM runs; the box score agrees with agent-continued grades (rank correlation at least 0.7) in at least half the decision families; a skilled scripted policy from a poor start beats a weak policy from a rich start under position-relative scoring.
cheap_score_paths: Steer into states where the correction's value function misjudges luck. Blocked: each correction term is zero-mean whatever the value function, so steering changes variance, not the expected score [inference; proof check needed].
Make decisions that look good under the scripted continuation. Blocked: decision grades are diagnostics, not the headline, and the agent-continued audit drops families where the two grades disagree.
Behave well only at graded moments. Blocked: moments are sampled at hidden random times, and doing nothing is graded too.

Gamble on high-variance strategies. Blocked: the correction removes world luck, not strategy risk; the ruin, CVaR and log-wealth panels remain, and the design report's rules for defaulted runs still apply.
Win by starting rich. Blocked: scores are relative to scripted results from the same start.
Submit the best of many runs. Blocked: the gateway logs every run that starts, and all of them count.
directions.fit_with_design_report: REUSES: the world tape, keyed draws, forkable daily state store and verifier replay; the R1 reference ladder, which becomes the value function and the continuation policy; the settlement and continuation value (already a frozen-reference rollout); the cluster bootstrap and the variance-components pilot; the starting-position dimensions in D08 §2.5. CHANGES: (1) draws must be keyed per event, not per day, or alternatives shift later draws; (2) adds a CPU rollout service and a correction step to the verifier; (3) the headline value added is computed on luck-corrected settled equity; (4) the power plan (25-40 scenarios x 2-3 seeds) is re-sized once the variance cut is measured; (5) adds rich/poor duplicate starts as a scenario dimension (the report says only that 'starts rotate across scenarios'); (6) the same fork machinery serves Directions 1 and 2 (probe truth and twins are both forks), so this is shared infrastructure rather than a rival plan.
risks: AIVAT has already been applied to LLM poker agents (AV-AIVAT, PokerSkill) [S], so the claim must be 'first in a long-horizon business simulation', not 'first for LLM agents'.

The gain may be small if world luck is small. Prosus's scripted operator varies only about +/-5% across seeds, and the design report guesses that most variance comes from the agent's own sampling (D08 §1 item 6) [speculative]. The CPU pilot must measure world luck's share first. If it is low, the value rests on decision grading, which is the less validated part.

Unbiasedness assumes the agent cannot see a batch of draws before the correction point, and that draw distributions that depend on the agent's state are computed exactly. This needs a written proof and red-teaming.
Decision grades depend on the continuation policy, so multi-step plans can still be misgraded despite the audit.
It is the least headline-friendly of the three ('we removed luck' is a methods story). It probably works best as the engine under Direction 1 or 2 rather than as the public identity.

directions.name: Duplicate Shop League (working title): same world, unequal seats
directions.one_line: Every entrant runs the same seeded shop worlds ('boards') from each of 3–4 unequal starting seats: a well-funded incumbent, a newcomer with little runway, and a struggling business taken over with a bad lease. Each entrant is scored on value added over par for that seat, so the hand it was dealt cannot win for it.
directions.capability_measured: Business judgement relative to position: choosing and carrying out the right plan for the position you are in (defend, grow, conserve cash or cut losses) in a world that is identical for every entrant. INDEPENDENT variables (we set them): (1) the entrant: a model, or a model plus its harness in a separate track; (2) the seat, drawn from D08 §2.5's start dimensions: cash runway 1–12 months, site traffic ×0.5–2, reputation 3.0–4.8 stars with 0–500 reviews, debt 0–12 months of revenue, lease fit, regulars, equipment age; (3) the board, meaning the world-tape seed. HELD CONSTANT: tools, context policy, effort tier, horizon, counterpart kernels and every outside random draw. DEPENDENT variables (we measure them): value added on settled equity over the seat's par (the headline); survival, ruin and worst-seat score; a seat-adaptation index, which asks whether the agent's policy shifts between seats in the same direction as the oracle's [design, untested]; conduct per opportunity; tokens and dollars.

core_facets.plain_meaning: As in duplicate bridge, every entrant plays exactly the same world: the same customers, weather, supplier behaviour and shocks. Random draws are keyed to events, so the world stays the same whatever the agent does. Each result is compared only with results from that same board.
core_facets.novelty_claim: No business benchmark uses 'result on this board minus par (or the field) on this board' as its headline. The seeded simulators (YC-Bench, CEO-Bench, E-Commerce Bench) still publish raw money averaged over runs [P via D11]. Project Deal ran parallel markets, but as a one-off study, not a league [P]. [inference, from one sweep]
core_facets.closest_prior_art: Project Deal: four parallel markets, Opus vs Haiku assigned at random, the same item compared across sellers [P]. Buyout Game: mirrored match packs, in a social game [P]. Supply_Chain_Bench: paired by seed and week, against one reference [P]. Business Arena: '10 matched runs' [P]. Event-keyed common random numbers (arXiv 2603.11084) and paired seeds (arXiv 2512.24145) [S].
