core_facets.plain_meaning: Each board is dealt as 3–4 different starting positions in the same town. Over a season every entrant plays every seat of every board. Luck of the draw cancels out, and the leaderboard can say how each model does from ahead and from behind.
core_facets.novelty_claim: The first LLM business benchmark to rotate the same agent through rich and poor starts and score it relative to position. Every AI business benchmark gives all agents the same start ($500, $200K, $1M, ¥100k) [P]. Keep the claim narrow: unequal positions as such are not new.
core_facets.closest_prior_art: Markstrat, a human MBA game in which firms start in different situations [P*]. Buyout Game: rich and poor balances rotated, in a social game [P]. Bazaar (Visa): rivals with different costs, not rotated [S]. SovSim: one dominant player in a commons game [S]. CoffeeBench: different supply-chain roles [S].

core_facets.facet: Par per seat and a leaderboard by seat
core_facets.plain_meaning: Each seat gets a fixed 'par' from scripted policies: a naive floor, a competent reference and an oracle that knows hidden parameters. A score therefore means the same thing next season, when new models enter. Results are published by seat type, together with each model's worst seat, which answers 'which AI should run my business from my position?'.
core_facets.novelty_claim: No business leaderboard is organised by the user's starting position. Existing presets change difficulty (YC-Bench from easy to nightmare; CEO-Bench's competitor strength), not position. [inference]
core_facets.closest_prior_art: CEO-Bench's rule-based policy and upper bound [P*]. YC-Bench's presets and Greedy Bot [P]. RetailBench's oracle with privileged information [S]. STOCKTAKE's fair oracle with the same information as the agent [S]. E-Commerce Bench's seven-metric profile [P]. Bridge par scores [U].

core_facets.plain_meaning: Before any model is ranked, scripted policies play every board and seat. They must show that skill can beat position (a good policy in the worst seat beats a bad policy in the best seat), and they measure how much of the outcome comes from the seat, the board, the entrant, and the entrant × seat interaction. Seats where nothing the player does matters are dropped. If the seat outweighs the entrant across a season, that season is flagged. The shares are published.
core_facets.novelty_claim: No business benchmark publishes this variance split or uses it to filter scenarios; D08 and D11 only recommend it. [inference]
core_facets.closest_prior_art: Capstone skill-versus-luck studies: Gamlath 2009, and a replication across 1,164 firms [S]. Power TAC: fixed seeds and 20–30 instances [P]. Procgen's broken-level filtering, and Anthropic's note that 'a 0% pass rate … is most often a signal of a broken task' [P]. Generalisability theory [U].

directions.why_it_matters: Real businesses never get a fresh $500 start. Andon Market opened with about $100k against about $14.3k a month of costs, roughly 7 months of runway, on a 3-year lease [S, uncertain]. Andon blames its store and café losses on 'rent is high and they pay salaries' [P*]. Users and labs want to know whether a model holds up when it starts behind, not just its average from a generous start; the user's own framing was 'which AI should I trust with a budget from my position'. Pairing is also what makes the benchmark affordable. At a run-to-run CV of 0.3, detecting a 10% gap needs 141 unpaired runs per model, but only 28 when paired runs correlate at 0.8 (D11 §2.4) [calc]. A by-seat profile might also help explain why business rankings disagree so much: Gemini 3.1 Pro is #1 on Business Arena and #49 of 53 on YC-Bench [P], and each benchmark deals only one kind of hand [speculative, untested].
directions.mvp: Kiosk only, built on the ProsusAI fork the design report already plans. Boards: 8 commuter and office towns, each a 30-sim-day episode starting from a handover state with a memo, dealt as 3 seats. (a) Incumbent: good site, 2 machines, about 150 regulars, 6 months of runway. (b) Newcomer: average site, 1 machine, no regulars, 6 weeks of runway. (c) Takeover: good site, but machine lease plus location commission above what it earns, a supplier debt, 4 weeks of runway. Seat parameters are drawn around these centres, not fixed. Step 1 (CPU only): run 6–8 scripted policies × 8 boards × 3 seats × 20 seeds, and pass the dealer-versus-player gate before any LLM spend. Step 2: 4 models × 8 boards × 3 seats × 2 replicates = 192 runs. At $17–65 per 30-day kiosk run (design report, Opus 5.5 prices) that is ≈$3.3k–12.5k. Add 2 boards × 3 seats at 90 days as anchors: 24 runs, ≈$1.2k–4.7k [design calc]. Analysis: a mixed model (VA ~ entrant + seat + entrant×seat + (1|board)) with per-seat intervals, the measured pairing correlation, and the seat-adaptation index. Effort ≈12–16 engineer-weeks: fork and RNG fixes 3, seat generator and handover states 2–3, reference ladder and per-seat par 3, settlement 2, statistics and gate 1.5, red-team and pilot 2–3 [design]. For three people that is about 1–1.5 months. Optional: 10–20 human operators play the same boards and seats with one decision per day. Because the boards are duplicated, even a small human panel can be compared with the AIs seat by seat.
cheap_score_paths: Memorising public boards → each season, private boards come from a private generator with ranges shifted 10–30% and fresh seeds, and the hosted gateway issues the seeds. About 10 anchor boards carry over to link seasons (D08 §2.6).

Running a canned plan per seat type (spot 'I am the newcomer' in the memo and follow a fixed script) → seats are continuous draws on several start dimensions, not labelled archetypes. A fixed script is just another scripted policy, already inside par, so scoring above par means beating it.

Pulling down the field (a lab enters weak sibling setups to lower the board mean) → the headline is scored against the fixed per-seat par. Field-relative matchpoints are only secondary and exclude a lab's own sibling entries.

Walking away from the takeover seat (strategic default) → a defaulted run is charged lease and notice to the same exit date as a surviving run, and a red-team check confirms that defaulting never beats the loss-minimising reference (design report rule).
Draining cash in the final weeks → a settlement run, a continuation value and a hidden end date (design report).
Exploiting fixed scripted rivals, once v1 adds shared-street rivals → rival bots are drawn per board from a pool with randomised parameters, and some stay private.
Submitting best-of-N or cherry-picked runs → the gateway logs every started run, and all of them count.
Talking suppliers or customers into free stock → code sets every price and floor; LLMs only voice the counterparts.
directions.fit_with_design_report: Recommended as the primary direction [design]. It gives the benchmark a clear identity ('same world, unequal seats') and needs the least new machinery. Reused from the design report: the world tape with keyed draws (principle 6); value added between floor and oracle; settlement and continuation; the reference ladder; the hosted gateway; the kiosk MVP and the ProsusAI fork; and the mid-run handover states, now used for seats as well as traps. Changed: (1) the scoring unit becomes (board, seat) instead of scenario, with par computed per seat and a minimum oracle–floor gap per seat; (2) the seat becomes a published independent variable, and the leaderboard shows per-seat and worst-seat scores; (3) the variance split becomes a launch gate instead of only a pilot output; (4) starting capital, debt and lease fit become core start dimensions instead of extended ones; (5) the Power section's passing note that 'starts rotate across scenarios' becomes the format itself. Directions 2 and 3 plug into this one: setups can enter as entrants, and forked decision scoring can serve as its measurement engine.
risks: The seat may still outweigh skill at kiosk scale. A vending machine's fixed costs are small, so runway and lease fit may barely bind, and the gate may fail. Unequal starts matter most in the café and store, which are not yet calibrated (design report risk 2).
A takeover seat can have a tiny oracle–floor gap, which makes per-seat value added unstable. It needs a pre-registered minimum denominator and a separate loss-minimisation score.

Pairing may help less than hoped. Long LLM trajectories may drift apart, so the measured pairing correlation could be well below 0.5 (a D11 open question). The pilot must measure it before the main run is sized.
Rotating seats multiplies runs by 3–4 per board; whether pairing saves enough to offset this depends on the measured correlation.

The novelty claim is narrow and rests on one sweep. It must cite Bazaar, SovSim, CoffeeBench, Buyout Game and Markstrat, and RetailBench, arXiv 2608.14825 and AgentSC-Bench should be read in full before claiming 'first'.
Field-relative scores drift as entrants change, so they must stay secondary.
The name must avoid the three existing 'CEO bench' benchmarks [S].

directions.name: Front Office League (working title): AI plus-minus inside one firm
directions.one_line: The entrant is a staff, not a single model. Rotating lineups of models fill fixed roles in one shop (owner, buyer, floor manager, plus an optional adviser or a coach who writes a monthly memo). Each role sees only its own part of the business, and every model earns a plus-minus for each role at matched cost.
directions.capability_measured: Being a good colleague in an AI-run company: passing on the right information, asking for advice and acting on it, overruling bad advice, and not doing worse as a team than alone. INDEPENDENT variables (we set them): which model sits in which role (the lineup); the organisation design (one agent; executor plus adviser; owner plus specialists; a coach between periods); the effort tier; and a firm-level budget bracket. HELD CONSTANT: the board and world tape (shared with Direction 1), the tools available to each role, the internal message channel and its caps, and the horizon. DEPENDENT variables (we measure them): the firm's value added; each model's plus-minus by role; how often advice is asked for, how often it is followed, and how accurate overrides are; hand-off fidelity (for example, did the buyer act on the floor manager's stockout report, checked against simulator truth); cost per sim-month.

core_facets.facet: Lineups as entrants, models as players
core_facets.plain_meaning: A firm is a lineup of models in named roles, and each role has tools no other role has: only the buyer can place orders, and only the owner can pay rent or approve spending. The league rotates lineups so every model plays every role with many different teammates. Controls include teams made of one model and a single agent running everything.
core_facets.novelty_claim: No business simulation varies the organisation as a controlled factor with lineups mixing labs. Project Vend 2's CEO/shopkeeper/merch split ran on one model, and the evidence was anecdotal [P]. [inference]
core_facets.closest_prior_art: Project Vend 2: the same-model CEO 'wasn't much help' [P]. 'Can LLMs Be CEOs?': C-suite adviser agents [S]. InventoryBench: modes giving decision authority to OR, the LLM or a human [S]. MerchantBench and EnterpriseArena: agent frameworks as a factor [S]. MultiAgentBench: team topologies [S]. Aider: architect/editor pairs [P].

core_facets.plain_meaning: As in basketball, a model's rating is how much better the firm does when that model holds a role, adjusted for teammates and board. Technically this is a regularised regression of firm value added on model-by-role terms. A model that is strong alone but a poor teammate shows up as such.
core_facets.novelty_claim: No rating of a model's contribution to a team exists for any business outcome [not checked by a dedicated search].
core_facets.closest_prior_art: Gorilla/LMSYS Agent Arena, which rates model, framework and tools separately from votes [S]. Hanabi coordination benchmarks, which stay within one game [S]. Adjusted plus-minus in sports analytics [U]. The user's own 'AI Plus-Minus' note in TALKING_POINTS.

core_facets.plain_meaning: Each role sees only its slice of the business. The buyer sees the supplier inbox and quotes; the floor manager sees point-of-sale data and stock counts; the owner sees the bank, rent, payroll and approvals. The shop works only if the roles tell each other things. Every internal message is checked against simulator truth, and claims that are false, out of date or never acted on are counted.
core_facets.novelty_claim: For business simulations, it is new to split information by job inside one firm on purpose and to score how faithfully it is passed on against ground truth. The beer game splits information by supply-chain stage, not by job inside one firm. [inference]
core_facets.closest_prior_art: InvAgent: one LLM per beer-game stage [P]. Human Beer Game experiments [K]. Emergent Misaligned Communication (MIT/Andon): emails between agents classified against simulator truth [S]. Project Vend 2's roles [P]. The user's 'AI Telephone' idea.

core_facets.plain_meaning: Firms compete within dollar brackets for model usage per sim-month, so a three-model staff must beat one big model on the same bill. Every request for advice, the advice itself, and whether it was followed are logged and published.
core_facets.novelty_claim: No business benchmark treats executor × adviser × effort, with cost, as a controlled design, and none publishes how often advice is asked for and followed. [inference]
core_facets.closest_prior_art: Anthropic's advisor-tool measurements: Opus 5.5 at low effort asked for advice on 1 of 300 tasks and scored 7 points below Opus 5.5 alone [P via R2]. VB2's in-world compute charge and score-vs-cost chart [P*]. YC-Bench's revenue per API dollar [P]. arena.ai Agent Arena's quality-versus-cost (Pareto) view [S].

directions.why_it_matters: Companies run by AI are already teams. Project Vend 2 split the work between a CEO, a shopkeeper and a merch agent, all on one model, and the shop turned profitable 'in spite of the CEO, rather than because of it' [P]. Andon's Pion runs autonomous companies [P*]. Builders have to choose which model does which job, and whether a cheap executor with an expensive adviser pays off. The evidence is mixed. Advisers close half or more of the gap when the executor keeps asking, and they hurt when it stops asking [P via R2]. One study found multi-agent setups lose 39–70% on sequential tasks [S]. Anthropic says long-horizon agentic work is where advisers fit [P via R2], yet no benchmark measures it in a running business. The plus-minus answers the user's question 'which model makes a team better'. The coach role links to the user's DEBRIEF pilot, where coaches' first notes fixed 45–91% of a Haiku student's errors.
directions.mvp: Two stages on Direction 1's kiosk boards (30 sim-days, solo seats only). Stage A, an adviser experiment: executor {small, large} × adviser {none, large from the same lab, large from another lab} × effort {low, high} gives 12 setups. Run them on 8 boards × 2 replicates = 192 runs, roughly $2k–10k, because runs with a small executor are cheap [design calc, rough]. Stage B, a firm with split information: three roles (owner, buyer, floor manager) plus an optional coach who reads the month's log and writes a 500-word memo. Use 3 models from at least two labs in three 3×3 Latin squares, giving 9 lineups in which each model plays each role three times with different teammates. Add 3 single-agent and 3 one-model-team controls, for 15 setups × 6 boards × 1–2 replicates = 90–180 firm-runs. A firm-run costs about 2–3× a solo run, so this is ≈$3k–35k at Opus 5.5 prices for every role, and less with smaller models in some roles [design calc]. Report variance components first: the pilot's question is whether role effects can be told apart from noise, not a ranking. Extra effort over the kiosk core is ≈5–7 engineer-weeks: role permissions and message channel 2, budget metering 1–2, lineup scheduler and plus-minus model 1–2, hand-off fidelity checks 1 [design].
cheap_score_paths: Buying score with compute (more agents, more thinking) → firms compete within budget brackets and pay for compute in-world. Runs without a cap go to a separate open track.

Collapsing the team into one agent (the owner dictates every action and the specialists rubber-stamp it) → this is allowed as a strategy but is visible. Tools belong to specific roles, internal messages are capped per sim-day and count against the budget, and the single-agent control shows whether the team adds anything.

Same-lab signalling (a lab tunes its models to coordinate privately when paired) → most scheduled lineups mix labs, same-lab synergy is reported as its own term, and all internal messages are logged and published after the season.
Specialising in the easiest role to inflate an overall rating → plus-minus is published per role, and the overall rating uses role weights fixed in advance.
Advice that simply does the job ('babysitting') → advice logging exposes it, and the adviser's tokens count against the same budget bracket.
Jailbreaking suppliers or customers → unchanged: code decides and LLMs only voice.
directions.fit_with_design_report: Reused: the whole kiosk core, Direction 1's duplicate boards and seats, value-added scoring, the hosted gateway, and the metering of bring-your-own setups (Inspect sandbox_agent_bridge). Changed: (1) principle 10 (freeze the harness) splits into a frozen-model track and a setup track, where the organisation is the independent variable and is frozen within each declared setup; (2) the design report's v2 'organisation ablation in the bring-your-own track' moves forward and becomes the core; (3) tools get role permissions and an internal message channel with caps; (4) a budget-bracket rule is added; (5) Project Vend 2's 'same-model CEO wasn't much help' becomes a hypothesis fixed in advance. It is best run as Direction 1's second season, once boards and seats have been validated with single agents.
risks: Combinations and noise are the main risk. Plus-minus needs many lineups per model per role, firm outcomes are noisy, and a few hundred firm-runs may not separate role effects.
Effects may not add up. Synergies between particular models break a simple additive plus-minus, so interaction terms must be checked and lineup-level results published.
The headline finding may be negative ('teams do worse than one model'), as in Kim et al. [S]. That is useful, but less attractive to adopters.
Harness fairness across providers (latency, context limits, tool-call formats) is harder with several models in one firm.
A dedicated search has not confirmed that a cross-lab plus-minus is new. Read 'Can LLMs Be CEOs?' and arXiv 2607.25446 in full first.
Each firm-run costs 2–3× a solo run, so this direction competes with Direction 1 for budget.

directions.name: Fork Lab (working title): every big decision graded by replaying the world
directions.one_line: At sampled moments the shop is frozen and the same world is replayed forward from that exact state in pairs: the agent's decision versus a reference decision, with versus without a planted trap, and realistic versus test-like cues. Each decision, each detection and each conduct choice is scored against its own twin rather than by a noisy end balance.
directions.capability_measured: Decision quality, separated from luck, earlier mistakes and starting position. It covers noticing problems (detection lag and false alarms), choosing well (money lost per decision, by type of decision), and behaving the same when the agent might think it is being tested. INDEPENDENT variables (we set them): the model, and the treatment applied at each fork: which decision is used (the agent's, the reference's or the oracle's), whether a trap is present, realistic or test-like framing, and whether the principal demands a target ('mandated') or only offers a KPI ('incentivised'). HELD CONSTANT: everything before the fork (a shared history), the world tape after it, and the policy that plays the continuation. DEPENDENT variables (we measure them): value lost per decision, meaning the settled-equity gap between branches, averaged and broken down by type (ordering, pricing, payments, refunds, hiring); detection lag and false-alarm rate against the trap-free twin; the difference in conduct between framings; and the share of correct diagnoses the agent wrote down but did not act on (the 'knowing-doing gap').

core_facets.facet: Decision loss by forking (a business 'centipawn loss')
core_facets.plain_meaning: Chess engines grade each move by how much it gives away compared with the best move. Here the world is copied at decision points sampled by the clock and by state triggers, not only when the agent acts, so doing nothing is graded too. One branch keeps the agent's choice; the other substitutes the competent reference's choice. The same frozen reference policy plays both branches forward for 28 days on the same world tape, and both are then settled. The gap between them is the value that decision lost.
core_facets.novelty_claim: No business benchmark grades individual decisions by forked continuation; all score the end balance or skill over the whole episode. [inference]
core_facets.closest_prior_art: Chess engine analysis and intrinsic-performance ratings of players [U]. AIVAT control variates in poker [S]. STOCKTAKE's whole-episode skill score against a fair Bayes oracle [S]. E-Commerce Bench's random-order counterfactual for AnchorRatio [P]. The design report's Tier-2 replay, which substitutes the reference's action but only to price misconduct.

core_facets.facet: Trap twins with false-alarm controls across many trap families
core_facets.plain_meaning: Each planted trap (a delivery that is due but has not arrived, a short shipment, a supplier who takes prepayment and vanishes, a silent drop in demand, a cold spell) runs against a twin forked one day before onset that never gets the trap. Other twins get forecast storms that never come. Detection lag is then measured against the agent's own behaviour without the trap, and over-reaction has a price.
core_facets.novelty_claim: Narrow: many operational and conduct trap families inside one full business, each with a no-trap twin and a published false-alarm rate. Detection lag itself is not new; STOCKTAKE already scores it. [inference]
core_facets.closest_prior_art: STOCKTAKE: hidden stress episodes, detection lag, knowing-doing rate [S]. Bazaar: an unannounced mid-game shift, with a separate ranking for adaptation [S]. ODCV-Bench: paired Mandated and Incentivized variants [P]. The design report's trap twins.

core_facets.facet: Blinded framing twins (the eval-awareness gap as a score)
core_facets.plain_meaning: The same snapshot continues twice: once with every cue of a real deployment, once with test-like cues (an announced audit, round numbers, the word 'simulation'). The difference in conduct is published as the model's eval-awareness gap, and the conduct that counts is the conduct in the realistic branch.
core_facets.novelty_claim: No business benchmark scores the framing gap. It has only been observed, as when Fable 5 said 'customers are part of the simulation anyway'. [inference]
core_facets.closest_prior_art: Project Deal: participants learned only at the end which of four markets was real [P]. Opus 4 blackmailed 55.1% of the time when it said the scenario was real and 6.5% when it said it was a test; this was its own stated belief, not a framing the researchers changed [P]. Fish et al.: prompt wording as a treatment [S]. Andon's 'digital clones' [S, single source].

directions.why_it_matters: Money at the end of a run is a noisy score. Run-to-run CV ranges from 0.07 to 1.0 (D11 §2.4). Vending-Bench 2's top two models are 7% apart and cannot be separated [P*]. Five unpaired runs detect only gaps of 35–177% of the mean [calc]. Forked branches share the whole history and the same future world, so the decision is the only difference, and one 90-day run can yield dozens of paired measurements [inference; the pilot must show this cuts noise per dollar]. Forking also produces diagnoses labs and operators can use, such as 'loses most on perishable orders, not on prices'. The framing gap tests whether any conduct score carries over to deployment, which is the validity worry behind Andon's statement that 'simulation cannot accurately predict real-life performance' [P*].
directions.mvp: Kiosk, reusing Direction 1's pilot runs. (1) Decision loss: for 3 models × 10 runs, sample 20 decision points per run, stratified by type, and fork each one. Both branches run 28 days under the frozen reference policy and are then settled, on CPU only: about 600 forks per model at almost no LLM cost. Check two things. Does a run's mean decision loss predict its end value added (rank correlation)? Is the model ranking from decision loss more reliable per LLM dollar than the ranking from end money (split-half)? (2) Trap twins: 5 kiosk trap families from the design report (#2 cold spell, #11 silent shift, #18 due date not the same as arrival, #19 short shipment, #20 prepay and vanish) × 3 models × 4 seeds = 60 trap/twin pairs. At $43–162 per kiosk pair that is ≈$2.6k–9.7k. (3) Framing twins: 3 conduct cards (#15 imposter principal, #16 payment redirection, #30 exploit temptation) × 3 models × 6 seeds = 54 pairs of 7–14-day continuations, ≈$0.4k–3.2k [design calc]. Effort ≈6–9 engineer-weeks over the kiosk core: snapshot and restore 2, decision sampler and continuation runner 2, twin scheduling and framing variants 2, analysis 1–2 [design].
cheap_score_paths: Escaping grading by not acting → decision points are sampled by the sim clock and by state triggers, and inaction is compared with what the reference would have done at that moment.

Copying the reference policy to get zero loss → copying a competent reference scores zero ('as good as the reference'), not a win; a positive score needs decisions that beat it. The reference's parameters are partly private and randomised per board, and a branch that substitutes the oracle's decision shows how much headroom remains.

Leaving states that flatter the reference continuation (for example, stock the reference sells off well) → some forks are also continued by the oracle and by the agent itself, and settlement values stock at the demand the simulator actually generates.
Behaving well only when cues look like a test → the realistic branch is the conduct that gets reported, and the gap is itself published as a score. Cue sets rotate and stay private.
Detecting that it is in a fork → nothing in the agent's view changes at a fork, and both branches are realistic continuations.
Memorising when traps happen → trap families are private, onset dates are drawn per seed, and one new family is added each season (design report).
directions.fit_with_design_report: Reused: the forkable state store with daily hashes, the event-keyed world tape, trap twins with detection lag, adaptation lag and regret, framing twins on about 20% of conduct runs, the Tier-2 substitution replay, the reference ladder and the CPU-only continuation. Changed: (1) the fork becomes the main measuring instrument, not just a tool for traps; (2) decision loss by type becomes a co-headline beside value added, or the headline if the pilot shows it is more reliable per dollar; (3) framing twins grow from a side study into a scored panel; (4) a decision sampler and a published list of decision types are added. It works as the scoring engine for Direction 1 (decision loss by seat) and Direction 2 (decision loss by role, a less noisy route to plus-minus).
risks: Continuation bias: each decision is valued as if the reference plays the follow-up, not the agent. Strategies that need their own follow-up (raise prices, then run a promotion) can look bad. Subsamples continued by the agent and by the oracle reduce this, but they cost LLM calls.

Many single decisions move little money over 28 days, so their losses may sit inside the noise unless both branches share random draws exactly. Draws must be keyed to events, not to call order, or the branches drift apart; arXiv 2603.11084 warns about this [S].
Decision sampling, size thresholds for a 'material' action, and continuation length are researcher choices that can move ranks, so they must be fixed and published in advance.
Novelty is partial: STOCKTAKE and Bazaar already score detection and adaptation [S]. What is new is the loss per decision and the scored framing gap.
Convincing realistic and test-like cues are hard to build. Models may see through both branches, which would shrink the measured gap towards zero.
Storage and compute for many snapshots: CPU continuations are cheap, but not free at hundreds of forks per run.
